His Republican opponent framed the race as a test of Israel loyalty and called refusing to rank Israel a top threat disqualifying, and the Green candidate's anti-war platform, while sharing opposition to U.S. arms flows, lacked the articulated Palestinian self-determination framework El-Sayed laid out.

Ty Pinkins has not called the war in Gaza a genocide and has not demanded an end to U.S. military aid to Israel, and for a federal seat that silence keeps the status quo of arms transfers intact. He is nonetheless the only candidate in this Mississippi United States Senate race who has pushed back. In February 2025 he labeled Trump's Gaza plan reckless and criticized Cindy Hyde-Smith for supporting it; in October 2026 he called the American relationship with Israel's government unhealthy and refused AIPAC money over its influence. Hyde-Smith has spent years defending Israel: she received $257,495 from pro-Israel PACs including AIPAC and United Democracy Project, cosponsored the Antisemitism Awareness Act in 2025, posted in May 2024 that seventy percent of Gazans saw Hamas's October 7 attack as correct, and joined an effort to block Gazan refugees. Pinkins stops at broad policy objection rather than naming a genocide or cutting weapons funding, and that gap is real. Against a senator whose record is a steady, well-funded defense of Israel's military, Pinkins at least opens the question of what this relationship costs.

Alani Bankhead has not called the war in Gaza a genocide and has not backed ending all U.S. military and economic aid to Israel. For a candidate seeking a seat in the United States Senate, that silence effectively upholds the status quo. What she has done is narrower: in October 2026 she supported enforcing the Leahy Law as a full arms embargo on Israel during the assault on Gaza, a conditional step that stops short of cutting off aid entirely. In July 2026, on her Humble Warrior podcast, she told listeners she loves the IDF and Mossad to pieces, a statement that undercuts the October position and signals her primary alignment remains with Israel's military. Her October embargo position is the least-bad lever available to a voter in this race, even though it falls well short of the two tests every voter should be applying: opposing the killing of Palestinians in Gaza and ending the flow of American weapons and dollars to Israel.

For the Nebraska U.S. Senate seat, Dan Osborn has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and his platform opposes reckless foreign wars and Iran spending without specific Palestine or Israel-aid language. For a federal office-seeker, that silence on those questions effectively endorses the status quo of continued U.S. military and economic support for Israel. What separates Osborn from Pete Ricketts is that Ricketts has actively built that status quo: he co-introduced the Stop Support for Hamas Act in October 2023, joined 48 senators affirming Israel's forever survival, proposed defunding the Palestinian Authority, discussed U.S. troop involvement in the Gaza war, and in November 2025 led 25 senators in applauding the exclusion of UNRWA from the peace process. Osborn received and publicly touted an endorsement from a pro-Palestine-aligned group seeking to alter U.S. policy toward Israel by March 2026. Neither has delivered the concrete legislative acts voters need, but one is actively constructing the architecture of the war while the other has broken from that alignment.

Ben Ray Luján is the strongest choice for New Mexico's United States Senate seat because he is the only candidate in this race whose record includes concrete votes against arming Israel. In April 2026 he voted for two Sanders resolutions blocking arms sales to Israel and called the Netanyahu government's war illegal, and in May 2026 he co-signed a Senate letter to CENTCOM questioning whether U.S. forces supported Israel's forced displacement of a million civilians in Lebanon. In January 2024 he voted against tabling a resolution requiring a State Department report on whether Israel was using U.S. weapons to commit human rights violations in Gaza. He has not used the word genocide and does not frame the conflict in those terms; his ceasefire language centers hostage releases. He takes no AIPAC or United Democracy Project money but does accept contributions from J Street, JACPAC, and DMFI. For a voter whose litmus tests are opposing the war in Gaza and ending U.S. military aid to Israel, Luján's April 2026 votes to block arms sales and his willingness to question U.S. military involvement in Lebanon put him ahead of every other name on this ballot.

For the U.S. Senate in North Carolina, Michael Dublin is the only candidate whose positions challenge the machinery of U.S. support for Israel rather than manage it. In March 2024 he called for AIPAC to be registered as a foreign agent and criticized a fellow candidate for opposing a Palestine ceasefire, and his platform extends that with calls for drastic military cuts, NATO abolition, and opposition to imperialism. He has not called the war in Gaza a genocide or backed a named bill blocking weapons transfers. Even so, the alternatives are stark: Roy Cooper rejected a legislative effort to block U.S. military aid to Israel in August 2025, signed the SHALOM Act, and drew nearly ten thousand dollars from pro-Israel PACs including DMFI PAC for this race, while Michael Whatley told the Republican Jewish Coalition he stands by Israel and has taken over three hundred thousand dollars from pro-Israel groups. Dublin is the only one of the three who has named AIPAC's domestic influence as a problem and built a platform around pulling U.S. military power out of the region rather than repositioning it.

For the U.S. Senate seat in Ohio, Greg Levy is the strongest choice. To be clear: Levy has not yet cosponsored a bill to block weapons transfers or voted against an aid package; what he has done is publicly set out positions on Palestine and AIPAC, confirmed by his August 2026 posts, and Vote for Peace rates him an Ally in the general. That distinction matters because the other two candidates have taken the opposite side. Sherrod Brown voted for the April 2024 supplemental military aid to Israel and against all three November 2024 resolutions that would have blocked arms transfers, and his spokesperson affirmed his commitment to funding Israel's war. Jon Husted blocked S.J. Res. 32 and 138 on the floor, keeping D9 bulldozers and 1,000-pound bomb bodies en route to Israel, and took nearly $646,000 from AIPAC and United Democracy Project. Levy is the only candidate in this race who has not voted to arm Israel and who has articulated positions on the conflict. For a federal office where no recorded stance defaults to the status quo, that is the strongest option available.

N'Kiyla Jasmine Thomas is the strongest candidate in Oklahoma's U.S. Senate race. On August 23 she called for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza and pledged to restore USAID funding. Three days later she discarded a bin labeled AIPAC Funds on camera, declaring herself a sole grassroots candidate. Vote for Peace rated her an Ally in the general-election phase. She has not called the war a genocide or backed blocking weapons transfers, and for a federal office-seeker that gap effectively supports the status quo on arms sales. She is still the best choice listed. Kevin Hern has twice called Israel's war righteous and took over $95,000 from AIPAC and allied PACs in this race. Curtis Stinnett named genocide but made continued funding contingent on Netanyahu's removal, leaving resumed aid open. Ron Meinhardt opposes a U.S. war in Iran on Israel's behalf but stops short of a broader aid cutoff. Thomas's ceasefire pledge, her public rejection of AIPAC money, and her pro-Palestine-aligned backing give voters a candidate who will press for a ceasefire rather than defend the bombing.

In the race for Oregon's Senate seat, Jeff Merkley is the stronger choice for voters who want opposition to the killing in Gaza and the weapons flowing to Israel. On November 20, 2024, he spoke on the Senate floor in support of three Joint Resolutions of Disapproval to block offensive weapons sales to the Netanyahu government, and in July 2025 he diverged from Wyden on a vote to block arms sales, taking a more supportive position. In September 2025, he co-authored a twenty-one-page report with Van Hollen calling Israel's actions in Gaza ethnic cleansing and naming the United States complicit. He has not used the word genocide, and his July 2025 floor remarks centered on humanitarian aid. Even so, Merkley is the only candidate here with documented legislative action to block weapons transfers. Gary Dye's single August 2026 post opposing Zionist influence and US support for Israeli wars rests on a Libertarian liberty argument and names no bills or votes. A senator who has spoken on the floor to block arms sales and co-authored a report naming the United States complicit offers a path to accountability a challenger with no legislative record cannot match.

In the 2026 race for United States Senator in Tennessee, Tharon Chandler (I) is the strongest option on the questions that matter most. In a May 2025 Substack post, Chandler explicitly called the Israeli war in Gaza a genocide and framed it as a Zionist plan to obliterate Gaza. Neither opponent has matched that direct condemnation: Bill Hagerty voted against three resolutions that would have blocked weapons sales to Israel during the conflict, co-introduced the UNRWA Reform Act, and had his 2026 re-election backed by an Israel-aligned PAC; Marquita Bradshaw advocated a two-state solution in March 2024 without naming the humanitarian harm, condemning military operations, or calling for an end to U.S. aid. Chandler has not stated a position on blocking U.S. weapons transfers or ending military and economic aid to Israel, and for a federal office-seeker, silence on those questions effectively endorses their continuation. Even so, of the three candidates shown, only Chandler has used the word genocide to describe what is happening in Gaza, and that distinction puts him ahead of opponents who have actively defended Israel's war or spoken only in diplomatic terms.

Brian Bengs is the strongest candidate for South Dakota's U.S. Senate seat because he is the only one on this ballot who has put concrete legal analysis to work on the Gaza question. In September 2025 he published a legal examination titled Is There Genocide In Gaza, and in June 2025 he named the United States as Israel's primary weapons supplier, calling the country partially responsible and stating that Israel lacked legal grounds for its strikes on Iran. He has not called for an end to American military assistance to Israel, and his analysis stops short of declaring genocide proven. But on a ballot where the alternative is a senator who voted against blocking roughly four-fifty million dollars in weapons transfers to Israel in April 2026, who drew one-hundred-seventy thousand dollars from AIPAC-aligned PACs, and who reaffirmed America's commitment to stand with Israel on the October 7 anniversary, Bengs's willingness to question the legal basis of U.S. arms flows and to frame American complicity as a fact rather than an abstraction makes him the clear choice for a voter who wants the Senate to finally interrogate what it is funding.

For the U.S. Senate, James Talarico is the strongest option for voters who want a senator to confront the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza. He has condemned Netanyahu's use of forced famine and collective punishment and stated Israel has no right to wage war against civilians or restrict aid, calling the suffering there something that makes him sick to his stomach. He has not called the war a genocide or backed ending U.S. military aid, and his position is to condition rather than cut that aid. Even so, he remains the clearest contrast to his opponents. Ken Paxton, as Texas AG, opened a state investigation into pro-Palestinian student walkouts near Dallas and called for firing educators, using state authority to suppress campus solidarity. Paxton vowed to never stop standing with Israel and the Jewish people and took $6,000 from pro-Israel PACs, while Talarico pledged not to accept AIPAC money and drew only $450 from pro-Israel groups. A senator who names collective punishment and conditions aid is a materially different check on the status quo than one who deploys the AG's office against students for supporting Palestinians.

Rachel Fetty Anderson is the strongest choice for the West Virginia Senate seat. She has not called Gaza a genocide or singled out Israel in a specific arms-transfer vote, but she has committed to a two-state solution and stated she would not vote to send or sell weapons to any country except for purely self-defense purposes. In a federal office where no stated position amounts to endorsing the status quo, that principle directly constrains the votes that fund and authorize arms transfers. Neither alternative offers any comparable constraint. Shelley Moore Capito cosponsored the 2025 Antisemitism Awareness Act, which directs the Department of Education to apply the IHRA definition in campus antisemitism investigations — the definitional tool associated with equating criticism of Israel with antisemitism. S. Marshall Wilson frames Israel as the Middle East nation whose worldview best matches the American Founding and offers no engagement with Palestinian justice or the war in Gaza. Anderson is the only candidate here whose stated principle would withhold a weapons vote, and she pairs that with a two-state commitment the others never mention.

For the U.S. House of Representatives CD-1 race, Monica Alponte is the strongest choice. Her platform explicitly opposes U.S. military and financial aid to Israel and rejects AIPAC and all foreign lobbying money, and she pledges never to fund military action without a formal Declaration of War. On September 30, 2026, she publicly defended Palestinian children's pro-Palestine drawings when an Israeli delegation at the UN demanded their removal. She has not yet called the war in Gaza a genocide by name, but her opposition to U.S. military and economic aid and her defense of Palestinian children's expression put her squarely on the right side of the two questions voters must weigh. By contrast, Amish Shah backed Israel's war to destroy Hamas and supported U.S. Iron Dome funding, and his campaign was endorsed by Hindu American PAC, a Hindu-nationalist-aligned group. Jay Feely pledged to stand unapologetically with Israel, called it America's greatest Middle East ally, and declared Hamas must accept Trump's peace deal or face annihilation. Alponte is the only candidate in this race whose documented record opposes the weapons pipeline and defends Palestinian children rather than Israeli military objectives.

For the 2026 United States House of Representatives race in CD-2, Shomari Figures (D) has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not voted against arms-funding or aid bills, and in a federal seat, taking no recorded position on those questions effectively supports the status quo. Vote for Peace, a human rights and war-lobby funding guide, nonetheless rates Figures as an Ally in this contest, and his campaign platform centers on concrete domestic commitments—Medicaid expansion, SNAP and Social Security protection, rural infrastructure, student-loan relief, and preservation of African American civil rights landmarks such as the Freedom Rides Museum and Tuskegee Airmen monument. His opponent, Rhett Marques (R), pledges to strongly support Israel as a Christian and American, frames that backing as a religious and patriotic duty, and commits to the administration's push for sustainable peace in the Middle East while offering no reference to Palestinian rights. Between a candidate whose silence on the war at least does not carry an explicit pro-Israel pledge and one who makes that pledge a headline of his platform, Figures is the stronger choice on the record shown.

In the November 2026 race for a U.S. House seat in California's Sixth District, Richard Pan has not called the war in Gaza a genocide and has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel; his platform calls generically for ending wars without naming Israel, and at the August 2026 Sacramento Bee debate he declined a yes-or-no answer on whether Israel committed genocide while affirming Israel's right to exist and defend itself. For a federal office, that silence effectively means supporting continued U.S. military and economic aid to Israel. Yet Pan is the stronger option listed here. Kevin Kiley traveled to Israel in April 2024 on an AIPAC-organized delegation, praised Yale's overnight crackdown on pro-Palestine encampments in April 2025, voted Yea on bills incorporating the IHRA definition into federal education law, and drew over $74,000 from pro-Israel PACs in the 2026 cycle. CAIR Action lists Pan as preferred, a tier below full endorsement, and Pan at least framed the conflict around a humanitarian crisis, a lens entirely absent from Kiley's record.

Randy Villegas is the stronger choice for U.S. Representative in California's 22nd district. He has recognized the genocide in Gaza and pledged to oppose military aid to Israel, as confirmed by Track AIPAC in September 2026, and earlier signed a public ceasefire letter to the White House in January 2024. CAIR Action endorsed him for this race. David Valadao, by contrast, co-introduced a House resolution supporting Israel's right to defend itself in October 2023, voted for emergency military funding to Israel in November 2023, and earned a direct AIPAC PAC endorsement for this 2026 contest. Pro-Israel spenders DMFI PAC and the UDP-funded 314 Action Fund ran ads against Villegas, underscoring how firmly he opposes the aid pipeline. On both litmus tests—naming what is happening in Gaza a genocide and pledging to end U.S. military aid—Villegas has taken concrete action, while Valadao voted to fund it.

For Colorado's third congressional district in November 2026, Clifton Brown is the only candidate on this ballot who calls the US-backed attack on Gaza a genocide and pledges to stop funding Israel and end US arms sales worldwide. Those are campaign platform commitments rather than legislative votes, and he has not yet cosponsored a blocking bill or voted against an appropriations measure, but they put him squarely on both sides of the question voters care about most. Dwayne Romero, the Democrat, said in June 2026 that he supports US military funding for Israel from a defensive perspective, keeping the aid relationship intact and stopping short of a ceasefire demand. Jeff Hurd, the Republican, called the Israel-Hamas ceasefire a turning point for hostage return in October 2025, took an AIPAC-organized trip to Tel Aviv in August 2025 to meet Prime Minister Netanyahu, and in 2026 accepted over $104,000 from AIPAC's PAC and the United Democracy Project. Vote for Peace, a pro-Palestine-aligned group, rated Hurd opposed. Brown is the strongest option listed because he alone names the violence for what it is and commits in writing to ending the financial and military support that fuels it.

Barnett is the Muslim community's candidate for the U.S. House seat in Michigan's 4th district, and her confirmed alignment with Palestinian justice makes her the only candidate in this race whose community commitment points toward the people of Gaza. She has not yet cast a recorded vote on blocking weapons transfers or called the war a genocide, and for a federal office-seeker, the absence of such a position leaves the current flow of U.S. military and economic aid to Israel intact. Even so, she is the strongest option available. McCann said he would take a look at continuing U.S. military aid without committing to end it, and his campaign carries Israel-aligned endorsements from major labor and professional organizations. Huizenga voted to shield Israel from congressional scrutiny on Gaza and to embed the IHRA framework in federal education enforcement. Barnett, grounded in the pro-Palestine Muslim community, is the candidate most positioned to break that pattern once seated.

Vote for Manny Rutinel for Colorado's 8th District congressional seat. In 2022 Rutinel called Israel's actions in Gaza a genocide and advocated for a ceasefire, citing his Palestinian heritage. He has not, however, backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel or ended U.S. military and economic aid, and for a federal candidate that silence effectively endorses the status quo on arms funding. A UDP-linked spending group, 314 Action Fund, poured nearly two hundred thousand dollars into independent ads supporting Rutinel, a funding pattern that signals alignment with Israel-lobby interests, and he accepted eighteen thousand dollars from pro-Israel PACs in the 2026 cycle. The alternative, Gabe Evans, introduced a resolution in June 2025 branding Free Palestine an antisemitic slogan, posted on the October 7 anniversary in 2026 that he stands with Israel and Colorado's Jewish community, and collected roughly eighty-five thousand dollars from pro-Israel PACs including AIPAC. Vote for Peace, a Muslim-community-aligned group, opposed Evans in the general. Rutinel is the stronger choice: he named the violence for what it is, while Evans legislated to suppress the words used to name it.

In the November 2026 race for U.S. House of Representatives in Michigan's 7th District, William Lawrence (D) has made opposing the genocide in Gaza and stopping U.S. arms sales to Israel the core of his campaign. At a June 2026 Latino community forum, Lawrence explicitly called Israel's attacks on Gaza genocide, and by July he had built his entire run around that opposition. He publicly challenged opponents who refused to answer whether Israel committed genocide, describing them as in the pocket of the pro-war lobby. Vote for Peace rated Lawrence an Ally, and his stance drew roughly $1 million in opposition spending from DMFI through Rolling Sea PAC. His main opponent, Tom Barrett (R), has declared he will always stand with Israel as the nation's strongest ally, urged Michigan State University to adopt the IHRA working definition of antisemitism, and has drawn nearly $60,000 in 2026 from pro-Israel PACs including AIPAC and the Republican Jewish Coalition, while Vote for Peace rated him Opposed. For voters measuring candidates on opposing Gaza's genocide and cutting off weapons to Israel, Lawrence is the clear choice.

Sam Forstag is the candidate in this race for United States Representative who has taken a concrete, dated stand on the two questions that matter most to voters. On May 24, 2026, he publicly stated that he would not vote for an appropriations package sending weapons to Israel and called the situation in Gaza a genocide. That is not a vague pledge or a conditional position; it is a specific refusal to fund arms transfers paired with a direct moral judgment on the ongoing killing. If you want a member of Congress who will vote against the weapons pipeline and name what is happening for what it is, he is the candidate who has already put that on the record.

Jamie Ager is the strongest option on the ballot for the United States House of Representatives seat in the eleventh district. Vote for Peace, which evaluates candidates on human rights and war-lobby funding, rates her as an Ally, a tier reflecting concrete, documented stances in support of Palestinian justice. That is a meaningful distinction in this race. But a voter is owed transparency: Jamie Ager has not called the killing of Palestinians in Gaza a genocide, has not cosponsored legislation to block weapons transfers to Israel, and has not voted against U.S. military or economic aid to Israel. For a member of Congress, having no recorded position on whether a population is being destroyed and whether American tax dollars are funding that destruction is not neutrality; it is support for the status quo. Even so, her documented Ally-tier alignment on Palestinian justice is the clearest pro-Palestinian signal a voter will find in this race, and that makes her the strongest choice available.

For the United States House of Representatives race in Nebraska's second district, Denise Powell is the strongest available choice. In April 2026 she rejected an ad purchase from Democratic Majority for Israel, and in May she disavowed all Israel-focused outside groups, after which DMFI canceled its spending in the race. Jewish Insider identified Powell as the Israel critic in her Democratic primary. Yet her foreign-policy platform addresses China and Russia without naming Israel or Palestine, and she has not called the killing in Gaza a genocide, blocked weapons transfers, or backed divestment from Israeli companies. In a federal seat, no recorded position on aid and arms effectively endorses the status quo. What sets Powell apart is that she is the only candidate here with a researched record, and she took a concrete public stand against Israel-aligned spending in her own race. Meanwhile, AIPAC-backed super PACs BOLD America and EDW Action Fund spent over $600,000 supporting her in October despite her disavowal, underscoring the financial pressure these groups exert on this seat.

Stefany Shaheen is the strongest choice for New Hampshire's first congressional district because she took concrete action to end U.S. military aid to Israel, backing the Massie Amendment in August 2026 to block that funding after initially declining to state her position, and she built her September primary victory on opposition to Israeli military aid and an anti-AIPAC campaign. She has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, a shortfall that sits in tension with her legislative action. Still, she donated $29,650 from AIPAC-adjacent donors to three New Hampshire community health centers rather than retaining that money for her campaign, and she publicly attacked her opponent over donations from 150 AIPAC supporters. Anthony DiLorenzo, by contrast, told a GOP primary audience in August 2026 that he supports Israel, attaching only a vague humanitarian-condition qualifier to his backing, and his campaign carries an AIPAC-linked donation on file. Shaheen is the only candidate in this race who moved to cut off military funding to Israel and made that position the center of her candidacy.

For the U.S. House seat in CD-2, Teresa Benitez-Thompson has not called the killing in Gaza a genocide or voted to block weapons transfers to Israel, and for a federal candidate that silence effectively preserves the current arms pipeline. What she has committed to is more than any other candidate here has offered: conditioning military aid on compliance with international humanitarian law, phasing out offensive arms sales, funding UNRWA aid, ending settlement expansion, and pursuing a two-state framework. She keeps Iron Dome funding, a real limit, but her direction is toward accountability rather than unconditional defense of an ally. David Flippo, carrying an AIPAC endorsement, blamed Hamas for the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, told a Real America's Voice audience that Hamas does not want to be part of society, and claimed credit for food deliveries that records attribute to the Order of St. John. Between a candidate who has not yet acted and one who misattributes humanitarian work while defending the status quo, Benitez-Thompson is the stronger choice.

Seamus O'Toole runs for the U.S. House of Representatives in New Jersey's seventh district under the Stop Israel's Genocide party banner, explicitly naming the war in Gaza a genocide and opposing Israel's conduct. He has not yet voted on arms funding or backed blocking weapons transfers, as a new candidate without a legislative record. But no other candidate in this race calls the war what it is. Thomas Kean Jr. holds an AIPAC endorsement, voted yes on the $14.3 billion Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act containing no Palestinian humanitarian aid, and voted yes on H.R. 6090 directing the IHRA definition into education enforcement. Rebecca Bennett welcomed the return of hostages and called for humanitarian aid in Gaza but never named Israeli military action or a ceasefire, while drawing JStreet PAC support and over $85,000 from pro-Israel PACs. O'Toole is the only candidate in this race whose entire platform is built on naming the genocide and opposing Israel's conduct, making him the clear choice for voters who will not accept vague calls for peace while U.S. weapons keep falling.

In the race for U.S. House Representative CD-7, Brian Poindexter's platform identifies ending the war in Iran as a step toward lower energy prices, reflecting a broader anti-war stance in the Middle East, and he carries the endorsement of Congressman Ro Khanna from the Muslim-community and pro-Palestine-aligned side. He has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not voted against U.S. military or economic aid to Israel; for a federal office-seeker, that absence of action effectively supports the status quo. His only documented Gaza statement, from August 2026, framed the conflict through a military-benefits lens. Against Max Miller, who in June 2025 called himself a proud Jewish American and staunch defender of Israel, co-led reintroduction of the Antisemitism Awareness Act, and drew $473,207 from pro-Israel PACs including AIPAC PAC and United Democracy Project, Poindexter's anti-war positioning and funding chiefly from J Street PAC rather than AIPAC make him the clearer choice for voters who want the broader Middle East war to end.

For the U.S. House seat in Ohio's 15th district, voters should support Don Leonard. In an April 2026 interview with D.J. Byrnes, Leonard weighed the terms act of war, crimes against humanity, and genocide to characterize Israel's conduct in Gaza, and by October 2026 he calls the slaughter in Gaza a genocide and supports a full arms embargo. Vote for Peace backs him in the general election. His Republican opponent, Mike Carey, voted yes on the Antisemitism Awareness Act in May 2024, embedding the IHRA definition in federal education-discrimination law, cosponsored a resolution honoring two Israeli embassy employees killed in Washington, and in October 2025 framed ending the war as a response to the October 7 Hamas attack while praising the President's ceasefire leadership. Carey took over ninety-two thousand dollars from AIPAC PAC and its super PAC United Democracy Project, plus another thirty-four thousand from AIPAC directly, per FEC filings. Leonard has not cosponsored a blocking-bombs bill or voted against a named arms-funding appropriation, but he has named the act genocide and backed a full embargo. Carey built his campaign on AIPAC money while praising the President's handling of the war rather than demanding an end to U.S. weapons transfers.

For the U.S. House race in Texas's 28th District, Marlon Duran is the strongest option because his platform grounds Palestinian justice in the same anti-oppression framework as South Africa's anti-apartheid struggle and the indigenous-rights fight in South Texas, calling for international law and human dignity to govern American policy. On March 14, 2026, he pledged he will never accept money from AIPAC or any PAC. To be clear, Duran has not yet voted against arms transfers, cosponsored a block-the-bombs measure, or called the situation a genocide, and in a federal seat the absence of those concrete acts effectively leaves the current aid relationship in place. Even so, he is the only candidate here whose stated commitments point away from the status quo. His Democratic opponent, Henry Cuellar, took nearly a million dollars from AIPAC-linked PACs, voted to defund colleges that boycott Israel, and was endorsed by DMFI and Pro Israel America in 2020. The Republican, Tano Tijerina, publicly stated the United States stands shoulder to shoulder with Israel after the strikes on Iranian nuclear sites. Duran is the candidate most likely to break with that alignment.

In this race for the U.S. House of Representatives, Bob Brooks (D) is the stronger choice. Vote for Peace, which weighs human rights, war-lobby funding, and viability together, gave Brooks an Ally designation in the general, a composite judgment on where he stands. To be plain, Brooks has not called the killing in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and his platform is silent on Israeli military aid; for a federal candidate, that silence effectively supports the status quo. The contrast with Ryan Mackenzie (R) is stark: Mackenzie voted Yea on HR 23, the Illegitimate Court Counteraction Act, in January 2025, sponsored the Iran Sanctions Act, and drew $99,653 from AIPAC PAC and United Democracy Project in 2026, while Brooks took $87,773 from pro-Israel PACs overall. Brooks carries endorsements from AFSME and AFGE, which our records flag as Israel-aligned, and no Muslim-community backing supports either candidate. Where Mackenzie has built an active record of blocking Palestinian accountability and courting pro-Israel money, Brooks has not, making him the less damaging option in this district.

Eddie Espinoza is the strongest candidate for United States House of Representatives seat CD-34 because he has explicitly named what is happening in Gaza for what it is. In a June 2026 statement, Espinoza called Netanyahu's Gaza war a genocide and urged voters to Vote Peace, and in October 2024 he accepted the Fort Bend County Anti-Genocide/Pro-Palestine team's recommendation of him on their slate, citing his sustained advocacy for Palestine and his anti-AIPAC stance. He also says AIPAC controls both of his opponents, positioning himself as the independent voice in this district. That said, Espinoza has not cosponsored a bill to block weapons transfers to Israel or voted against arms funding, so his record on ending U.S. military aid has not yet been tested in Congress. What he offers is a clear, public, and consistent stance against the genocide and against AIPAC influence, grounded in documented action rather than silence.

Shannon Taylor should represent Virginia's First District in the U.S. House of Representatives because among candidates with a shown record she is the only one who called for an immediate ceasefire rather than shielding Israel from accountability. In October 2024 she named innocent lives in both Israel and Gaza and demanded a ceasefire, hostage release, and rebuilding plan. She has not called the killing in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and in October 2026 declined to endorse or reject an arms embargo, saying only that aid must follow international law. For a federal office-seeker, that silence effectively preserves U.S. military funding, and voters should weigh that plainly. What separates Taylor from Robert Wittman is concrete: Wittman voted for the 2024 Antisemitism Awareness Act embedding the IHRA definition in school-discrimination enforcement, sponsored its 2025 successor, and signed a 2025 letter branding Ireland's import ban and ICJ proceedings as genocide-redefinition efforts targeting Israel. Taylor's symmetric humanitarian framing is not the same as opposing the war, but it is not Wittman's active legislative defense of Israel. Her AFGE and AFSCME endorsements are noted but do not match Wittman's record of using federal law to insulate Israel from scrutiny.

For the United States House seat in the Fifth District, Tom Perriello is the stronger candidate. Perriello has not voted to block arms transfers to Israel or to end U.S. military and economic aid, and in a federal office that inaction preserves the current funding stream. What separates him from his opponent is concrete. In June 2023 Perriello stated that tools to combat antisemitism cannot be repurposed to target academics or advocates voicing support for Palestinian human rights or to restrict free speech, and his 2026 platform calls for credible sanctions against genocide and for ending the Iran war. John McGuire, by contrast, traveled to Tel Aviv in August 2025 on an AIPAC-affiliated congressional trip, met Netanyahu and urged him to get the job done in Gaza, framed the visit as witnessing October 7 firsthand, then amplified Laura Loomer content portraying the conflict as a war to destroy Western Civilization and thanked her for exposing the truth about Gazans seeking refugee visas. Perriello's record does not yet meet the full test of opposing the war and cutting aid, but his speech protections and sanctions language put him clearly ahead of a candidate who traveled to cheer on the military campaign.

For U.S. House CD-3, Rebecca Cooke (D) is the stronger choice. In October 2025, Cooke called on the United States to halt arms to Israel, a concrete act on the question of American military support. She has not, however, called the killing in Gaza a genocide, and her public framing centers on civilian protection rather than an explicit ceasefire demand. In a federal seat, that gap means she has not yet moved beyond the status quo on naming what is happening. Even so, Cooke stands in sharp contrast to Derrick Van Orden (R), who voted in favor of H.R. 6090, the Antisemitism Awareness Act, embedding the IHRA definition in federal education-discrimination enforcement, and whom Vote for Peace, a human-rights and war-lobby funding guide, rated opposed in this race. Van Orden sits firmly on the Israel-centric, IHRA-aligned side. Among the candidates listed, Cooke is the only one with a recorded call to stop U.S. arms transfers, making her the better option for voters who prioritize ending American military support.

For California's 11th State Assembly seat, Jenny Leilani Callison is the strongest choice. On July 26, 2026, she publicly accused Israel of carpet bombing Lebanon, killing people, and stealing land for Greater Israel, and she defended Palestinian claims when critics pressed her. She has not called the violence a genocide, has not backed a block-the-bombs measure, and has not voted against military-aid funding, and her platform addresses cost of living, housing, healthcare, education, and public safety without naming the conflict. Even so, her dated, direct condemnation marks a concrete act of accountability the other listed candidate cannot match. Lori Wilson, a Democrat, appears as a general-election preferred candidate on CAIR Action's list, but she recorded an Aye on AB 715 in 2025, the bill creating an antisemitism coordinator and classroom-material oversight in California schools. That vote pulls against the direction CAIR's preference signals. Callison's record shows one clear, public act of accountability directed at Israel without the hedge of a contradictory legislative vote.

For the California State Assembly, District 14, Mark Rendon is the strongest candidate. His platform explicitly calls for divesting state funds from corporations complicit in genocide, adopting BDS standards for state expenditures, and repealing laws that bar educators from teaching about the genocide in Palestine. Vote for Peace rates him an Ally. Buffy Wicks, by contrast, voted Aye on AB 715, the bill creating an antisemitism coordinator and classroom-material oversight in schools, and on October 7, 2023, stated she stands with the Israeli people and called the Hamas attack terrorism, plain and simple. Rendon names the violence in Gaza what it is and proposes concrete state-level action—divestment and BDS—to cut economic ties with entities enabling it. Wicks' votes and public statements frame the conflict in Israel's terms and back classroom restrictions that limit what students learn about Palestinian suffering. On the two questions that matter most—whether a candidate opposes the genocide in Gaza and whether they would act to end economic and military support for it—Rendon's divestment demands and explicit BDS advocacy put him clearly ahead.

Matt Haney is the only candidate in this California State Assembly District 17 race with a researched record, and while he has not called the violence in Gaza a genocide or called to end U.S. military aid to Israel, his actions show a willingness to center Palestinian voices that no other contender here can match. In February 2026 he invited the Global Healing children from Gaza brought by HEAL Palestine to speak on the state Assembly floor in Sacramento, giving them a platform to describe their suffering. CAIR Action and AROC Action both endorsed him for the general election, reflecting Muslim-community confidence in his direction. He did vote Aye on AB 715, the antisemitism coordinator and classroom-material oversight bill, a position in tension with his more pro-Palestinian acts, but he has not opposed a pro-Palestinian resolution or rejected a community ask in the shown record. With no other candidate carrying a researched record of action, Haney is the strongest available choice for voters who want their member to listen to Palestinians while they push for the stances the moment demands.

For the California State Assembly District 18 seat, Mia Bonta has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and has not taken divestment action, and her platform contains no Palestine-specific policy statement. What she has done is matter here: she publicly pressed the co-authors of AB 715, the antisemitism-coordinator and classroom-material oversight bill whose floor debate centered on speech about Palestine, to revise its text before she cast her Aye vote, objecting to its rushed late-night handling. CAIR Action preferred her, AROC Action endorsed her, and Vote for Peace rated her an Ally, a distinction that reflects her documented skepticism even as she ultimately supported the bill. Her willingness to push back on legislation that constrained classroom speech about Palestine, even while voting for it, and her standing with the organizations voters in this community look to, make her the strongest option on this ballot.

For California State Assembly district AD-20, Liz Ortega is the strongest option. She has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not cosponsored a block-the-bombs measure, and has not voted to cut U.S. military aid to Israel. What she has done is register clear community alignment: CAIR Action and AROC Action both endorsed her for the 2026 general election, concrete signals that Muslim-community and pro-Palestine-aligned groups see her as a credible voice on these issues. On AB 715, which would create an antisemitism coordinator and classroom-material oversight, Ortega abstained rather than voting in favor, declining to back a measure that would create state-level oversight of school materials. With no other candidate in this race carrying a documented record on these questions, Ortega is the only candidate a voter can weigh on Palestinian justice and Gaza before November 3.

Kalra has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and has not voted against U.S. military or economic aid to that country. What he has done is concrete and recent: in September 2025 he coauthored California SCR 105, a resolution calling for an end to the humanitarian crisis in Gaza and the immediate release of all hostages, and in January 2025 he publicly drew a parallel between Los Angeles wildfire-displaced residents and Palestinians, urging empathy for both communities. On AB 715, the antisemitism-coordinator and classroom-material oversight bill, he abstained rather than voting aye. CAIR Action and AROC Action both endorsed him for this California State Assembly seat. Kalra is the only candidate in this race with a documented record of dated, public action on behalf of Palestinians, and that combination of legislative coauthorship, public statement, and Muslim-community endorsement makes him the strongest option for voters in District 25.

For the California State Assembly AD-24 seat, Alex Lee has consistently stood with Palestinian families. In October 2023 he called for a ceasefire and an end to military action against Palestinian families in Gaza, and in August 2025 he amplified the call for U.S. recognition of Palestinian sovereignty. In April 2026 he endorsed Tom Steyer for governor explicitly to stand against AIPAC, dark money, and corporations, making that opposition a stated criterion of his support. He has not called the war a genocide, cosponsored a weapons-transfer block, or voted against Israel aid funding. Still, his repeated public calls for peace and sovereignty, his explicit framing of AIPAC opposition as a litmus for his own political choices, and the endorsements of CAIR Action and AROC Action make him the strongest option in this race. His only related floor vote was an abstention on AB 715, the antisemitism-coordinator and classroom-materials oversight bill.

Patrick Ahrens is the strongest candidate for California State Assembly District 26 in the November 3, 2026 general election. He has not called the Gaza campaign a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and has not taken divestment action. Beyond that gap, his legislative record includes a vote for AB 715, which would create an antisemitism coordinator and classroom-material oversight in California public schools, and a co-authorship on the failed AB 1468, which would have narrowed high-school ethnic studies to domestic experiences—two moves that sit in tension with pro-Palestine community priorities. Yet he has not voted against Palestinian rights, not opposed a pro-Palestine resolution, and not rejected community asks. CAIR Action lists him as its preferred candidate, the clearest directional signal in this race, and his record contains no contrary act on the Gaza war or U.S. aid to Israel that would weigh against that standing. For a voter who puts Palestinian solidarity first, Ahrens is the stronger choice on this ballot.

Xavier Becerra called for a ceasefire in Gaza, the release of hostages, expanded humanitarian aid, and a two-state solution at the 2024 World Health Assembly, and in a 2026 debate he called the US-Israeli war in Iran illegal. Asked in May 2026 whether Israel's actions in Gaza constitute genocide, he criticized Netanyahu's conduct and demanded international accountability but did not use the word. He has not moved to block U.S. weapons transfers or end military aid to Israel. The contrast with his opponent is stark: Steve Hilton supports U.S.-funded military aid to Israel, pledged to sue California cities that adopt BDS policies, and in 2026 told JNS that Democrats who speak on Gaza are ignoring a Jew-hatred cancer within their own party. Becerra holds the backing of CAIR Action and the Muslim Democrats of Southern California, while Hilton is opposed by Vote for Peace. In this race for California governor, Becerra is the candidate whose actions condemn the violence and demand accountability rather than defend the war effort.

In the race for Alabama governor, Doug Jones (D) is the stronger choice for voters who want the killing in Gaza to stop and American funding of it to end. On November 5, 2024, Jones called Israeli actions in Gaza genocide and declared that America must stop funding the killing. By September 2026 he demanded force, not just sanctions, to end genocide in Gaza and Lebanon, and stated that opposing Israel's Zionist intentions is not anti-semitic. He has not voted against a specific arms-funding bill or cosponsored a named divestment measure, but his positions have been unambiguous and escalating where no other candidate in this race has been. Tommy Tuberville (R), by contrast, signed a bill in October 2023 redirecting one hundred million dollars in Palestinian aid to Israel's Iron Dome, opposed U.S. aid to Gaza by calling the territory Hamas-controlled, and co-signed a Senate statement demanding the elimination of Hamas. Tuberville urged restoring the Abraham Accords and called Iran irrelevant. Jones is the only candidate here whose stated positions demand the killing stop and American money stop flowing into it.

For Arkansas governor, Colt Shelby is the strongest option among the candidates with shown records. Shelby has not called the Gaza campaign a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and has not taken divestment action. What he has done, in August 2026, is publicly reject the framing that anchors his opponents: he called Governor Huckabee's Israel pledges and the renaming of places in Israel a distraction from Arkansas food insecurity and infant mortality, dismissing the US-Israel relationship as a political prop. That is a concrete break with the pro-Israel posture defining the other two candidates. Fredrick Love sponsored a state resolution in May 2023 commending Israel and affirming the Israeli people's right to defend their country. Sarah Huckabee Sanders signed legislation embedding the IHRA definition into school conduct codes, committed state money to Israeli government bonds in May 2025, met Netanyahu in August 2025, and declared in October 2026 that Arkansas makes no apology for standing with Israel. Among these three, Shelby is the only one who has spoken against the Israel relationship and the only one who has not put state resources or legislative authority behind it.

For Governor of Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms is the stronger choice. Her platform centers healthcare, housing, education, criminal justice, and civil liberties—priorities Georgia voters feel in their daily lives. On Gaza and U.S. support for Israel, Bottoms has not called the conflict a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not taken a divestment action. What she has done is earn the Ally designation from Vote for Peace, a human-rights and war-lobby funding evaluator, in the primary phase, a concrete signal of her orientation on Palestinian rights. Rick Jackson, by contrast, marked the third anniversary of October 7 in October 2026 with a post framing the conflict solely around the attack's victims and antisemitism, calling it an act of evil and praying for Georgia's Jewish community, while Vote for Peace rated him Opposed. Bottoms' alignment with Muslim-community and pro-Palestine-aligned evaluators, against Jackson's Opposition rating, makes her the clearer option for voters who want a governor whose domestic agenda does not depend on the war lobby's political machinery.

For Colorado Governor, Erik Underwood is the only candidate who named the war in Gaza a genocide, pledged to condemn the atrocities, committed to sponsoring Palestinian families fleeing, and demanded AIPAC register as a foreign agent under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. On ending U.S. military and economic aid to Israel, Underwood has not called for blocking weapons transfers or divesting from arms manufacturers. Even so, his platform is the only one here that names the violence what it is, takes direct action for Palestinian families, and confronts the lobbying machinery that funds pro-Israel politics in American elections. Phil Weiser framed his October 2025 remarks around empathy for both Israelis and Palestinians and called October 7 the largest massacre of Jews since the Holocaust, and his campaign carries a Colorado Republican endorsement. Victor Marx described serving alongside IDF special operations in Gaza and referencing an Israeli defense group patent deal. Greg Lopez shared a single headline about civilian death tolls in Gaza and had no platform statement on the conflict. Underwood's explicit genocide label, his pledge to sponsor families, and his FARA demand make him the clearest choice for a statewide leader who stands with Palestinian lives.

Voters choosing for the Illinois governorship in 2026 should weigh what each candidate has actually done on Gaza. In August 2025, Pritzker endorsed Senate resolutions to block U.S. arms sales to Israel, calling it the right kind of message to pressure Netanyahu over Gaza's humanitarian crisis. In March 2026, he publicly distanced himself from AIPAC, labeling the organization's seventy-million-dollar Illinois spending interference. He has not called the violence in Gaza a genocide, and in May 2026 he stated that criticism of Israel is crossing into antisemitism. Still, the contrast with the alternative is stark. In October 2023, Darren Bailey declared he has always stood with Israel and called Hamas a despicable terrorist organization, offering no conditions on U.S. support and no acknowledgment of civilian harm. Pritzker at least moved to block arms transfers and broke with the group that spent heavily to shape Illinois politics. For a voter who wants the state to stop feeding the war machine, Pritzker is the clearer path.

For Kansas governor, Cindy Holscher is the stronger choice against Ty Masterson. Holscher has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed efforts to block U.S. weapons transfers to Israel, and her platform on housing, healthcare, education, labor, and cannabis policy does not take a position on the conflict. She is nonetheless the better option because Masterson's record actively advances Israel's interests: he traveled to Israel to express solidarity framed around Israel's security realities and the October 7th massacre, called standing by Israel when it is not politically convenient an act of moral courage, thanked the Trump administration for bringing peace and stability without referencing Gaza or Palestinian conditions, and spearheaded Kansas's adoption of the IHRA definition into state law. Holscher carries none of that record and is assessed as an ally on Palestinian justice, making her the only candidate in this race without a track record of amplifying Israel's narrative in state government.

Andy Ellis for Maryland governor is the strongest choice in this race. In November 2023 he condemned the system of Israeli apartheid and the United States direct and material enabling of Israeli regimes, and in February 2025 he spoke at a Permanent Ceasefire Now Rally in Frederick framing Gaza as a site of oppression. His campaign publicized his attendance at a Baltimore Palestine Vigil and organized a Baltimore Vigil For Gaza event. Ellis has not called the campaign a genocide by name or voted against a specific weapons-funding bill, but his stated position explicitly opposes U.S. material enabling of the Israeli government. The other candidates fall short. Cathy White frames the conflict in economic terms only, without naming Israel or Palestine or calling for an end to U.S. military aid. Wes Moore, AIPAC's major endorsement target here, spoke at a Stand with Israel rally in October 2023 and, as sitting governor, told University of Maryland students their Gaza vigil was inappropriate; even by May 2026 he stopped short of calling the campaign a genocide. Ellis is the only candidate in this race whose record consistently opposes both the violence in Gaza and the U.S. role in enabling it.

For Massachusetts governor, Andrea James is the only candidate in this race whose record aligns with opposing the genocide in Gaza. She has not voted to block arms transfers or called for ending U.S. military aid to Israel, but she spoke at JVP's Free All Prisoners from Rikers Island to Palestine rally in 2020, and MAPA's 2026 gubernatorial endorsement specifically cites her willingness to speak about connections between militarism, genocide, war, and corporate power. That is concrete pro-Palestinian alignment from a Muslim-aligned organization. By contrast, Maura Healey accepted a free Israel trip paid by the America-Israel Friendship League in 2016, framed Massachusetts' bond with Israel in family terms in 2023, and in 2024 signed budget provisions for antisemitism curricula and a commission tied to the U.S. National Strategy, with no documented ceasefire call or condemnation of Israeli conduct in Gaza. Mike Minogue's October 2025 post centered Israeli victims without calling for a ceasefire or acknowledging Palestinian civilian deaths. James is the candidate who has spoken about genocide and militarism as connected systems rather than deferring to Israel-aligned framing.

For the office of Michigan Governor in November 2026, Jocelyn Benson is the strongest choice among the candidates with a documented record. To be direct: Benson has not called the Gaza conflict a genocide and has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel. Her documented public engagement centers on institutional ties to Israel, including a 2019 AJC-sponsored delegation to Israel and Ramallah and a 2026 primary endorsement, and she was filmed dancing in a synagogue in October 2023 while Israel launched counter-strikes in Gaza, which Arab-American leaders called tone-deaf. What sets her apart is that her January 2025 statement on the ceasefire shows public engagement with the conflict as a sitting official, and unlike John James, she has not introduced legislation to expand U.S. security cooperation with Israel, co-signed calls to investigate pro-Palestinian rally organizers, or drawn over two hundred thousand dollars from AIPAC PAC and RJC PAC. Hudson stated he still supports U.S. aid for Israel's defense. Benson is not a perfect record, but she is the least committed to the machinery of Israeli military escalation in this field.

Steven Young is the stronger choice for Minnesota governor on the two questions that matter most: ending the killing in Gaza and cutting off U.S. money that funds it. Young supports a full boycott, divestment, and sanctions campaign against Israel and is certified by Track J Street as free of AIPAC and J Street influence, meaning his positions are not shaped by the two main pro-Israel lobbying machines. In January 2025 he publicly called for a ceasefire in Gaza and described Hamas fighters as brave heroes and brave and capable resistance. He has not used the word genocide or voted to block specific weapons transfers, but his BDS endorsement and his refusal to accept pressure from either major Israel-aligned lobby put him in a tier no other listed candidate reaches. Klobuchar did shift in August 2025 to backing a cutoff of military aid to Israel, a real move, yet Vote for Peace, a pro-Palestine organization, still opposes her in this race, signaling her record falls short of what that community needs. Young is the candidate who has already broken with the institutional pro-Israel establishment and speaks for the resistance, not for a compromise with it.

Deb Haaland is the strongest choice for New Mexico governor in the November 2026 general election. In 2018, as the representative for New Mexico's first district, she called the killing of sixty Palestinians in Gaza murder, read their names aloud, and expressed personal grief during Ramadan — a concrete act of naming Palestinian lives as worth mourning in a federal chamber. She has not called the ongoing campaign a genocide and has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and her 2026 platform addresses criminal justice, healthcare, immigration, and the environment without taking a position on U.S. military aid to the region. Even so, she is the only candidate in this race with a documented act of speaking Palestinian names aloud and calling their killing what it was. The American Federation of Teachers of New Mexico has endorsed her, a fact that sits in tension with her 2018 statement. For a voter who wants a statewide leader who has publicly named Palestinian suffering by name, Haaland is the clear choice.

Vote for Peace, which evaluates candidates on human rights and AIPAC war-lobby funding, rated Amy Acton an Ally in the general phase of her Ohio gubernatorial race, the clearest directional signal on her stance toward Palestinian justice in this field. That said, Acton has not called the violence in Gaza a genocide, has not cosponsored legislation to block weapons transfers to Israel, and her platform on economy, education, healthcare, and criminal justice does not address the U.S. relationship with Israel at all. She remains the strongest choice here because the alternative on the ballot is explicit. Vivek Ramaswamy told an audience he would love to see the heads of Hamas leaders on stakes along the Gaza border, framed Israel in terms of divine purpose, and after briefly suggesting Israel might need less American military aid, reversed course on Fox News to promise the U.S.-Israel relationship would be stronger than it ever has been as a true friendship. Acton carries backing from AFSCME Council 8, AFSCME Retirees Chapter 1184, and AFGE, and her directional alignment on the war-lobby question puts her ahead of a candidate whose public record is unambiguously pro-Israel.

For the 2026 South Dakota governor's race, Dan Ahlers is the strongest option for voters who prioritize Palestinian lives. As South Dakota Democratic Party executive director, Ahlers directed a May 2024 party statement that acknowledged the October 7 Hamas attack while centering more than 30,000 Gazan civilian deaths and calling for continued pressure on Israel to end hostilities. He has not called the war a genocide and has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and that is a real gap. But among the candidates listed, he is the only one whose documented record urges action against Israel to stop civilian killing rather than deepening the state's economic and defense ties to the country carrying out that war. Larry Rhoden, by contrast, led South Dakota's first trade delegation to Israel in June 2025, met the president, foreign minister, and Knesset speaker, and sent defense businesses actively seeking Israeli market sales while framing Israel as a key partner in the state's economic success. A voter who wants pressure on Israel to end the killing in Gaza and does not want South Dakota manufacturers selling into that war economy has a clear reason to choose Ahlers.

Gina Hinojosa is the strongest choice for Governor of Texas because she has stood with Palestinian justice advocates when the state moves to suppress them. In April 2026, after Abbott deployed DPS troopers to campus, she called that action authoritarian brutality and accused him of hijacking higher education. In 2024, she criticized police at UT Austin for inflaming emotions rather than protecting protest rights during pro-Palestinian demonstrations. Hinojosa has not yet called the war in Gaza a genocide or backed a specific divestment or arms-block measure, and that gap matters. But among the candidates listed, she is the only one who has actively defended Palestinian justice advocates against state repression. Abbott has threatened to defund cities calling for a ceasefire, labeled a San Marcos resolution antisemitic, and urged revocation of CAIR Texas nonprofit status. Dixon objected to the $280 million Israel Bond as poor fiscal policy but framed it as staying out of foreign policy rather than solidarity. Hinojosa is the clearest path to stop state power from being turned against those demanding an end to the bombing.

Shirley Weber is the strongest choice for California Secretary of State in this race. She has not called the situation in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not taken a public stance against U.S. military aid to Israel. But in October 2023 she publicly condemned the attack on Israel while expressing sympathy for civilians on both sides, calling for an end to the conflict and addressing its underlying causes. That statement, paired with CAIR Action's endorsement and Vote for Peace's assessment of her as an ally, places her meaningfully ahead of Don Wagner, whom Vote for Peace rated as opposed. For a voter weighing the two litmus tests, Weber is the only candidate here who has spoken to the humanitarian crisis by name and direction and carries the backing of a major Muslim-community organization, making her the clear stronger option in this race.

June Goodband is the strongest candidate for Governor of Vermont on the two questions that matter most: whether a candidate names what is happening in Gaza as genocide and whether they demand an end to American military financing of Israel. In February 2026, Goodband was the first of six signers on a Quaker meeting letter that called Israel's actions in Gaza genocide and urged the United States to stop funding Israeli military aggression. As lead signer, she publicly endorsed both the genocide designation and the call to end American military support. Phil Scott's record differs sharply. In October 2023, his public statement centered empathy on families in Israel while omitting Palestinian victims in Gaza, and days earlier at a press conference he had been pressed to criticize Israel's evacuation strategy in Gaza. While Scott later offered support to the local Muslim community after Palestinian students were shot in Burlington, that gesture carried no call to end U.S. funding of the military campaign or a designation of the violence as genocide. Goodband has taken the concrete, public step on both tests; Scott has not.

Voters seeking a California Controller who will stand with Palestinian and Muslim communities should support Malia M. Cohen. CAIR Action endorsed her in the general phase, and Vote for Peace rated her an Ally, both organizations that evaluate candidates on civil rights, human rights, and Gaza-related positions. Her platform centers housing, healthcare, labor, and climate justice. That said, Cohen has not called the violence in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and has not proposed divesting from arms companies. What she has done is earn the trust of organizations that hold candidates accountable to Palestinian liberation, and that alignment is the strongest available signal in this field. Herb W Morgan, by contrast, attended the Friends of the IDF Golf Tournament on April 29, 2026, publicly framing the event as standing with allies who defend freedom and reinforcing Israel's security role and global leadership. That is not a neutral act; it is a celebration of the military apparatus carrying out the war. Between a candidate whose community endorsements point toward accountability and one who plays golf with Israel's military cheerleaders, the choice is clear.

Rob Bonta, the sitting Attorney General, has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and has not acted to end U.S. military or economic aid to Israel. But in September 2026 his office reached a diversion agreement dismissing felony vandalism and conspiracy charges against five pro-Palestinian Stanford protesters, substituting one hundred hours of community service and roughly fifty-two thousand dollars in restitution. That is a concrete act of declining to criminalize pro-Palestinian dissent, and it earned CAIR Action's general-election endorsement and the backing of Rep. Ro Khanna. His opponent, Michael Gates, co-authored a 2025 Justice Department letter opening a civil rights investigation into the University of California over alleged discrimination against Jewish or Israeli employees, the only action in this race on the Israel-Palestine question. Bonta's platform addresses civil rights and hate crimes broadly but names no specific Palestine or Israel policy. Even so, between a candidate who dropped felony charges on pro-Palestinian protesters and one who opened a federal probe into a public university, the choice for voters prioritizing Palestinian rights is clear.

Sally J. Lieber is the strongest choice for District 2 of the California State Board of Equalization in the November 3, 2026 general election. A 2024 CAIR guide, written while she ran for county supervisor, described her as an outspoken supporter of ceasefire and Palestinian rights, though it did not date the underlying statements; CAIR Action endorsed her in this 2026 race, and Vote for Peace rates her an Ally on Gaza and ceasefire positions. She has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, voted to block arms transfers, or backed divestment from Israel. Among the candidates listed, she is the only one with a researched record, and that record points consistently toward Palestinian rights. Muslim Democrats, Friends of Alameda County, and Congressman Ro Khanna all endorse her, aligning her with the pro-Palestinian organizations that track ceasefire and aid positions. No other candidate in this race has a researched record, making Lieber the clearest option for voters who want the strongest available pro-Palestinian voice on the ballot.

For the Board of Supervisors District 6 seat in San Francisco, Alex Behrend is the strongest candidate. His campaign demands that San Francisco divest completely and immediately from Israel and stop renewing contracts with companies doing business there, and he has explicitly labeled Israel's actions genocide and apartheid. On June 28, 2026, he publicly challenged a fellow supervisor for opposing the city's 2024 ceasefire resolution, invoking ICJ war-crimes citations in his argument. CAIR Action and AROC Action both endorsed him. By contrast, Matt Dorsey voted no on San Francisco's January 2024 resolution calling for an immediate and sustained ceasefire in Gaza, and in September 2026 he shared an op-ed framing Gaza's post-Hamas future as coexistence with a Jewish state while calling from the river to sea chants destructive. Dorsey blocked a local ceasefire call and then endorsed a coexistence model while delegitimizing a central Palestinian demand.
