For the Ward 4 Director seat on the Alameda-Contra Costa Transit District board in the November 2026 general election, Sarah Syed is the strongest choice among the candidates. She has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not voted against U.S. military or economic aid to Israel. What she has is a full endorsement from CAIR Action, a Muslim-community and pro-Palestine-aligned body whose recommendations weigh civil rights and foreign policy, including Gaza and ceasefire positions. That full endorsement, as opposed to a lesser Preferred designation, is concrete stance evidence that Syed aligns with Palestinian justice. No other candidate in this race carries a documented record of that kind, making Syed the only option on the ballot whose positions on Gaza and ceasefire have been vetted and affirmed by a community organization with direct skin in the game. For a voter who wants their transit board representative to stand with East Bay Muslim and pro-Palestine communities rather than stay silent, Syed is the clear choice.

For East Bay Regional Park District Director, Ward 3, in the November 3, 2026 general election, William Yragui is the strongest choice. He has not cosponsored a weapons-transfer ban, voted against arms funding, or publicly labeled the war in Gaza a genocide. However, CAIR Action endorsed him at its full endorsement tier rather than its lower Preferred level, and CAIR's process explicitly weighs civil rights and foreign policy, including positions on Gaza and ceasefire. That full-tier backing, alongside support from the Muslim Democrats and Friends Club, signals concrete alignment with pro-Palestine community priorities. Yragui's platform also addresses the governance voters will feel directly: wildfire readiness, trail access, habitat protection, and board transparency. He is the only candidate in this race with a researched record, and those Muslim-community endorsements give him directional evidence on the questions that matter most to this community.

Olivia Sanwong has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, or moved a divestment measure. What she does carry is a full-tier endorsement from CAIR Action, a Muslim-community organization whose recommendation process specifically weighs civil rights and foreign policy including Gaza and ceasefire positions, constituting a concrete assessment of her alignment with Palestinian justice. That full endorsement, not a softer preferred-level recommendation, signals that her overall record passes the two questions every voter should ask of this candidate: does she oppose the genocide in Gaza, and does she back ending U.S. military and economic support to Israel? For the Ward 5 Director seat on the East Bay Regional Park District board, Sanwong is the candidate with that Muslim-community backing behind her name. Vote Olivia Sanwong on November 3, 2026.

Vote for John Garamendi for California's Eighth District in the United States House of Representatives. Garamendi called Israel's actions in Gaza a genocide being committed against the people of Palestine in July 2025, signed the Block the Bombs Act, and said he voted against military support for Israel. He also demanded an end to the starvation crisis in Gaza and criticized the repeal of sanctions on violent settlers. In January 2026 he voted yes on an appropriations bill carrying $3.3 billion for Israel, a shortfall that leaves his record incomplete on ending economic aid. Even so, no other candidate in this race has a researched record on these questions, and Garamendi is the only one with documented action against the war. CAIR Action preferred him, and he takes no AIPAC or allied-lobby funding, while J Street PAC, a pro-Israel group, is the only tracked donor. For a voter who wants a member who has spoken plainly against the killing in Gaza and backed blocking weapons transfers, Garamendi is the strongest option in this field.

Mark DeSaulnier is the strongest candidate for the United States House seat in California's 10th district. In July 2025 he urged Israel to halt its military operations in Gaza, called the situation unacceptable by any standards of humanity, and stated he no longer votes for offensive military aid. He sponsored the Block the Bombs Act and voted against most Israel military-aid packages. He voted no in May 2024 on the Antisemitism Awareness Act imposing the IHRA definition in federal education enforcement. CAIR Action and J Street PAC endorse him; he has taken no AIPAC or UDP money. To be clear, he voted yes in January 2026 on an appropriations bill carrying $3.3 billion for Israel and against cutting $500 million in missile-defense funding, and has not called the war a genocide. No other candidate in this race has a researched record. DeSaulnier is the only one who has publicly broken with unconditional arms funding, moved from supporting to opposing offensive military aid, and drawn backing from both the Muslim community and a critical Jewish voice. On a federal seat where silence means the status quo stands, he is the only candidate who has moved.

For US Representative in California's 11th District, Connie Chan (D) has taken concrete steps on both litmus tests. In January 2024, as a San Francisco Supervisor, she voted with the 8-3 supermajority for a sustained Gaza ceasefire resolution. She has called the war a genocide, pledged to end all US military aid to Israel, fund no Iron Dome, and back a total arms embargo, and in a January 2026 interview she committed to co-sponsoring the Block the Bombs Act. Her campaign carries a standing pledge to refuse AIPAC money. She holds endorsements from Track AIPAC, CAIR Action, and AROC Action. By contrast, Scott Wiener (D) declined to call Gaza's destruction genocide when directly asked at a January 2026 debate, offering that language only in a follow-up video after sustained criticism. He had opposed local ceasefire resolutions, calling them fuel for antisemitism, and co-authored AB 715, a classroom-oversight bill CAIR California warned could censor Palestine teaching. Chan is the stronger choice for a candidate who has acted on ending the war and cutting off US weapons funding.

For the U.S. House seat in California's 12th district, Lateefah Simon has taken the most concrete legislative action to end American complicity in the genocide in Gaza. She cosponsored the Block the Bombs Act to halt U.S. arms transfers to Israel, voted to eliminate $3.3 billion in Israeli military aid, and in September 2025 publicly demanded an end to the genocide and passage of that arms-transfer bill, framing the crisis as U.S.-backed Israeli violence. Two contrary votes are on record—she backed a resolution conflating antisemitic violence with anti-Zionism and voted against cutting $500 million—but the weight of her record falls on the pro-Palestine side. Track AIPAC, CAIR Action, and AROC Action endorse her, and no AIPAC PAC money has reached her campaign. Jamie Joyce, the other Democrat, calls Gaza a genocide and refuses pro-Israel PAC money, but her framing targets Netanyahu as a war criminal rather than U.S. military support for Israel, and her 2026 pledge to end war does not specify an Israel or Gaza policy. Simon has moved legislation where Joyce has staked out positions.

For the U.S. House seat in California's 14th District, Aisha Wahab has taken concrete action on the two questions voters must weigh. In June 2026 she publicly called the situation in Gaza a genocide, in August 2026 she introduced a California Senate resolution describing the violence as genocide and calling for an end to the war, and she cosponsored the federal Block the Bombs Act to halt weapons transfers to Israel. Her opponent Melissa Hernandez declined at an April 2026 forum to call Israel's actions in Gaza genocide, and her campaign was propelled by $2.5 million from AIPAC's United Democracy Project plus $1.8 million from the UDP-funded Bold America super PAC. Wahab drew over $2.5 million in opposition from those same AIPAC-aligned groups and ran a campaign endorsed by CAIR Action and AROC Action. A candidate who names the killing of Palestinians what it is and backs legislation to stop the bombs is the one this district needs.

Sam Liccardo is the strongest choice for U.S. House Representative in California's 16th District because he has moved toward blocking U.S. weapons transfers to Israel. On July 14, 2026, he cosponsored the Block the Bombs Act, and in July 2026 he stated he will vote against the $3.3 billion in offensive weapons funding for Israel and against the larger appropriations package. In July 2025 he called for immediate humanitarian aid to Gaza and criticized U.S. military support for Israel's actions, and at an August 2025 town hall he validated residents' anger over Palestinian suffering. His record is not clean: he voted for a January 2026 appropriations bill carrying $3.3 billion in Israel aid, voted against the Massie amendment eliminating that funding, and still supports $500 million for Iron Dome and Arrow 3. He has not called the Gaza campaign a genocide. Yet CAIR Action endorses him, no AIPAC PAC or UDP support is reported on his behalf, and no other candidate in this race carries a researched record on these questions. For voters who want a representative working to stop the bombing, Liccardo is the only one with that documented effort.

For this seat in the U.S. House of Representatives, Ro Khanna (D) has moved most concretely on Gaza. He co-sponsored the Block the Bombs Act and a genocide-recognition measure, declared Zero Aid to Israel at a 2026 DNC meeting, introduced a June 2026 amendment to strike the U.S.-Israel military-integration provision in the NDAA, and in July 2026 co-sponsored a measure with Thomas Massie to block U.S. funding for Israel's military. He did, however, vote yea in January 2026 on an appropriations package carrying $3.3 billion in Israeli military aid, a vote that predates his subsequent push to strip that funding. His 2024 votes affirming Israel's right to exist predate this shift as well. Khanna carries endorsements from CAIR Action, AROC Action, and Track AIPAC; his only Israel-aligned backing is J Street PAC. His opponent Ritesh Tandon rejected the word genocide in October 2026, called a ceasefire demand naive in February 2024, and framed the conflict through an Israel-protective lens throughout. On opposing the war and ending U.S. arms transfers, Khanna's record shows active movement in a way Tandon's does not.

For the United States House of Representatives, Zoe Lofgren (D) is the strongest candidate in CD-18. She has sponsored the Block the Bombs Act and UNRWA-restoration legislation, called Gaza a humanitarian catastrophe, blamed Netanyahu for the famine, and urged a permanent ceasefire since October 2023. CAIR Action rates her a preferred candidate. That said, Lofgren has not called the war a genocide, has not sponsored genocide recognition, and she voted yes on fourteen billion dollars in weapons to Israel, the 2024 NDAA bundling military aid, an IHRA-based resolution, and a measure condemning the slogan from the river to the sea. Her campaign funding comes chiefly from J Street PAC with no AIPAC PAC or UDP money reported. She remains the best available choice because no other candidate in this race carries a researched record, and despite those contrary votes her sustained advocacy for a ceasefire, humanitarian aid, and a two-state solution places her on the pro-Palestinian side of the roster.

For the U.S. Senate seat in Colorado, Adam Withrow is the only candidate on the ballot who calls for an immediate halt to U.S. weapons transfers to Israel and frames the war as an extinction-level threat, while Hickenlooper voted in July 2025 with the Republican majority to defeat two resolutions that would have partially blocked military aid to Israel. Withrow has not called it a genocide or sponsored a specific blocking bill, but his Unity Party platform condemns the military harm and annexation and anchors peace in a two-state solution on pre-1967 borders. Hickenlooper's October 2025 ceasefire statement paired humanitarian aid for Palestinians with security for Israelis, and his FEC filings show he received $431,868 from pro-Israel PACs including $325,235 from AIPAC's United Democracy Project. Vote for Peace opposes Hickenlooper's candidacy. Withrow is the stronger choice for voters who want a senator working to stop the bombs rather than one who voted to keep them flowing while accepting AIPAC money.

For the United States Senate seat in Alabama, Everett Wess (D) is the stronger choice. Wess has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not taken a position on ending U.S. military or economic aid to Israel, and in a federal seat that silence effectively preserves the status quo of unconditional support. Even so, his 2026 platform calls for a ceasefire, humanitarian aid to Gaza, recognition of Palestinian rights, and a two-state solution. Barry Moore (R) stands with Israel, publicly supported funding to protect Israel, introduced the Define to Defeat Act extending the IHRA definition into federal enforcement, and drew money from AIPAC PAC and United Democracy Project. Wess does not frame the conflict around a hostage deal or hail a particular president as the peacemaker. He will not dismantle U.S. arms flows to Israel, but he is the only candidate here who has put Palestinian lives and a negotiated resolution at the center of a statewide platform.

Jon Ossoff is the strongest candidate for the United States Senate in Georgia on the war in Gaza. On April 15, 2026, he voted to advance resolutions blocking sales of military bulldozers and 1,000-pound bomb bodies to Israel, and in February 2025 he voted for resolutions blocking weapons sales, framing the vote as protest against disproportionate retaliation killing tens of thousands. In 2021 he led twenty-nine senators in a letter demanding an immediate ceasefire and has affirmed the IDF violated the laws of war. He has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, deferring that determination to the International Criminal Court, and his form-letter reply to a constituent's urgent genocide letter marks the limit of his positioning. Yet his concrete votes to block arms transfers stand in stark contrast to Mike Collins, who in September 2026 rebuked Ossoff for those votes, declared his faith compels him to support Israel, and drew nearly nineteen thousand dollars from AIPAC PAC and United Democracy Project. Ossoff took zero from those groups. Vote for Peace rates Ossoff an Ally and Collins Opposed.

For the Florida Senate seat, Angie Nixon is the only candidate in this race who has taken concrete action to stop the killing in Gaza. As Florida State Representative from Jacksonville, she introduced HR 31C in November 2023 calling for an immediate cease-fire, was the lone lawmaker to cite over ten thousand Palestinian deaths on the floor, and in 2026 called Netanyahu a war criminal who needs to answer to his crimes. She stated flat opposition to sending Israel any U.S. money or weapons, and her platform pledges to end U.S. support for West Bank settlements and impose human-rights conditions on aid. She has not used the word genocide, but her acts—backing a ceasefire, opposing weapons and funding, demanding a war criminal answer for his crimes—put her on the right side of history, as she told colleagues who turned their backs. By contrast, Ashley Moody voted against blocking arms transfers to Israel, co-sponsored a bill to cut UN agency funding over Israel, and raised over half a million dollars from pro-Israel PACs including AIPAC PAC. Nixon, endorsed by Ro Khanna, has stated she is not receiving AIPAC funding.

Vote for Matt Loesby for United States Senator in Idaho's November 3, 2026 general election. Loesby has not called the Gaza war a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not voted against aid bills; as a federal office-seeker, that absence effectively supports the status quo. What distinguishes him is direction against the alternative. In May 2024 he named the Neocon-Zionist faction and pro-Israel elements within the progressive coalition as a united force crushing those who support Gazan Palestinians, and in July 2026 he publicly questioned US political engagement on Israel-related foreign policy. His opponent Jim Risch has done the opposite on every front: in May 2025 he told the Senate floor that Gaza's suffering is Hamas's fault and the crisis is not Israel's, introduced the Senate NOPE Act to block UN funding for Palestine, co-introduced a bill to defend Israel at the United Nations, and in September 2025 formally opposed allied nations' recognition of a Palestinian state, calling Israel one of America's greatest allies. Loesby is the only candidate in this race who has spoken against the forces silencing Palestinian suffering rather than shielding the state responsible for it.

In the race for Iowa's United States Senate seat, Josh Turek is the stronger choice over Ashley Hinson. In September 2025, Turek backed conditions on U.S. support for Israel, a step that holds Israel accountable through conditional engagement. He has not called the killing in Gaza a genocide and has not backed blocking weapons transfers; his platform addresses civil liberties and immigration broadly but not a specific Israel-Palestine policy, and for a federal office-seeker that conditional stance effectively supports the ongoing status quo of U.S. military assistance. He also received $165,307 from pro-Israel PACs in 2026, chiefly from J Street PAC. Turek did draw Muslim-community and pro-Palestine-aligned backing from Rep. Ro Khanna. Hinson, by contrast, voted Yea on all three Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Acts in 2024, declared in August 2025 that Hamas is 100 percent to blame for the suffering in Gaza and that she will always stand with Israel, and in October 2026 defended her vote against a measure to end the Iran war. Turek's conditional posture, while short of a full break with U.S. military aid, places him on a different side of this question than a candidate whose record is defined by unconditional pro-Israel military alignment.

In the 2026 race for U.S. Senator from Kansas, Adam Hamilton is the stronger choice for voters who want an end to American bombs falling on Gaza. In an October 2026 POLITICO interview, Hamilton said he would vote to stop weapons transfers to Israel and end offensive military aid while preserving defensive weapons, explaining he does not want tax-funded bombs dropped on innocent people. He has not called Israel's actions in Gaza a genocide. His stated commitment to halting weapons transfers and cutting offensive aid stands in sharp contrast to Roger Marshall, who demanded immediate passage of a $14 billion standalone Israel aid package on the Senate floor in November 2023 and in May 2024 told Fox Business it was not the time or place to accept Palestinian refugees from Gaza. In April 2026, Marshall voted against a war-powers resolution requiring U.S. withdrawal from the Iran conflict. Hamilton's pledge to block offensive arms funding offers Kansas voters a clear alternative to a senator who has repeatedly pushed more American money and munitions into the war.

Charles Booker is the strongest choice for United States Senator from Kentucky in the November 2026 general election. At a televised primary debate on March 17, 2026, Booker called Israel's actions in Gaza a genocide and stated that the United States should not fund them. His campaign platform frames foreign policy around ending reckless wars, consistent with that explicit condemnation and his opposition to U.S. financial support for the campaign in Gaza. Vote for Peace, a pro-Palestine-aligned group, rated him an Ally heading into the general election. Booker has put his name on opposing the genocide and blocking U.S. funding, making him the clear choice for voters who want a candidate who will act to end that support.

Voters in Maine's 2026 United States Senate race should support Troy Jackson because he has called the war in Gaza a genocide and committed to ending U.S. military funding for Israel. At a September 29 town hall, Jackson stated Israel is committing a genocide, called Netanyahu a war criminal who should be prosecuted, and refused to vote for more bombs or aid. He reaffirmed the genocide label on October 1 and, at the October 7 debate, opposed giving a blank check to Israel, saying he did not want offensive weapons going to murder people in Palestine. Jackson also vowed before the July 2026 convention that he would never vote for U.S. taxpayer-funded military aid to Israel. His opponent Susan Collins cosponsored the 2025 Antisemitism Awareness Act, called current U.S. aid to Israel good in the October 7 debate, and drew the largest pro-Israel PAC contributions of any senator. Jackson carries endorsements from labor and retiree groups including the AFL-CIO and AFSCME, but it is his explicit, repeated commitment to opposing the genocide and cutting off U.S. aid that makes him the stronger choice in this race.

For the United States Senate seat in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed is the candidate who has put a Gaza ceasefire and ending U.S. military aid to Israel at the center of his platform. He called for an immediate ceasefire within days of the October 2023 attacks, again in February 2024, and after the al-Ahli hospital bombing in October 2023. His campaign frames opposing military aid to Israel as a core platform, and he has accused Congress of funding a military imposing genocide and mass starvation in Gaza. Backed by Congressman Ro Khanna, Organize for Peace, Jewish Voice for Peace Action, and Peace Action PAC, he drew over twenty million dollars in opposition from the AIPAC-backed super PAC United Democracy Project. In contrast, Republican Mike Rogers framed this race around Israeli victimhood, called El-Sayed's refusal to rank Israel above Iran as a threat utterly disqualifying, and treated a pro-Israel stance as a prerequisite for holding federal office. Green candidate Douglas Marsh also opposes U.S. weapons funding to Israel, but El-Sayed's articulated vision of self-determination for both Israelis and Palestinians and his broader coalition give him a clearer path to delivering results.

Peggy Flanagan is the strongest choice for United States Senator from Minnesota in November 2026 because she has taken concrete stands on the two questions voters must weigh first. On August 12 and 13, 2026, Flanagan publicly accused Israel of committing genocide and said she would have voted to cut off U.S. military aid to Israel. She also stated she would oppose offensive weapons sales to Israel and made Craig's AIPAC support a campaign issue. Ro Khanna, who endorsed Flanagan, aligns with Muslim-community and pro-Palestine-backed positions. By contrast, Michele Tafoya told a 2026 audience on October 16 that there is no genocide happening in Gaza, explicitly rejecting that characterization, and received donations from pro-Israel PACs in this cycle. For a federal office-holder, silence on these questions amounts to endorsing the status quo of U.S. arms transfers and aid, and Tafoya's platform contains no statement on Palestine or related humanitarian concerns. Flanagan is the only candidate in this race who has named the genocide, committed to ending military aid, and opposed offensive weapons sales.

For the United States Senate seat in Massachusetts, Ed Markey (D) is the strongest candidate. In April 2026 he voted to advance S.J. Res. 32 and S.J. Res. 138 blocking sales of military bulldozers and 1,000-pound bomb bodies to Israel and voted Yea to discharge a broader arms-export disapproval resolution. He co-signed a ceasefire appeal with 27 colleagues in May 2021, issued an official press release on arms-sale disapproval in April 2025, and in his September 2026 primary speech called to stop the bombing in Gaza and slash the Pentagon budget. He has not called the war a genocide in his own words, and his votes block specific weapons transfers rather than ending all U.S. aid to Israel. Still, among the candidates listed he is the only one with a floor record directly blocking arms to Israel. Joe Tache and Shiva Ayyadurai demand more sweeping cuts but run without a path to cast such votes, while John Deaton affirms Israel has the absolute right to defend itself and treats aid as a fiscal question. Markey took zero dollars from AIPAC PAC or United Democracy Project and holds the pro-Palestine endorsement of Ro Khanna.

Alani Bankhead for United States Senator in Montana. She has not called the violence in Gaza a genocide and has not backed a flat end to all U.S. military and economic aid to Israel. On her Humble Warrior podcast in July 2026 she said she loves the IDF and Mossad to pieces, and her October 2026 position frames aid as a Leahy Law arms embargo during the assault rather than eliminating transfers outright. That is a real step — it opposes continued arms shipments while the assault continues — but it stops short of the broader break a federal seat demands, and the earlier pro-IDF language complicates the record. For a statewide Senate race where silence on these questions amounts to endorsing the status quo, Bankhead is still the stronger option: she took a concrete, dated position against arms transfers, and the Leahy Law embargo, even as a conditions framework, puts pressure on the pipeline in a way a blank record does not. Voters who want a senator who will vote to stop the bombs outright may find her record incomplete, but among the candidates in this race she is the one who moved.

For the United States Senate, Ty Pinkins is the only candidate who has publicly challenged the direction of U.S. policy on Gaza. In February 2025 he called Trump's Gaza plan reckless and named Cindy Hyde-Smith for supporting it; in October 2026 he declared the American relationship with Israel's government unhealthy and refused to accept AIPAC money for his campaign. He has not called the war a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not proposed ending U.S. military aid, and for a federal office-seeker that absence leaves the status quo intact. Yet he remains the clear choice over Hyde-Smith, who in 2024 posted that 70 percent of Gazans viewed Hamas's October 7 attack as correct while joining an effort to block Gazan refugees from entering the country, and who has accepted $225,495 from AIPAC's own committee among more than a quarter million dollars from pro-Israel PACs. Pinkins has named the problem and turned away the money that funds it.

Dan Osborn is the strongest choice for Nebraska's U.S. Senate seat, though his Gaza record has limits. In April 2024 his campaign called Israel's response to Hamas justified, and his platform names no Palestine-specific policy; he has not called Gaza a genocide or backed blocking weapons transfers, and as a federal candidate, taking no recorded stance on these questions effectively endorses the status quo. But his trajectory and the contrast matter. By March 2026 he publicly touted an endorsement from a pro-Palestine-aligned group seeking to alter U.S. policy toward Israel, and his platform opposes reckless foreign wars and taxpayer spending. Pete Ricketts, by contrast, backed Israel's war and U.S. troop involvement in October 2023, proposed defunding the Palestinian Authority, co-introduced the Stop Support for Hamas Act, joined a resolution supporting Israel's forever survival, and in November 2025 led senators in excluding UNRWA from the Gaza peace process. Ricketts has repeatedly and actively deepened U.S. entanglement in Gaza. Osborn, an Independent, offers a clearer break from that record even as his own Palestine policy remains undeveloped.

Ben Ray Luján, the Democrat running for United States Senator in New Mexico, is the strongest candidate in this race for voters who demand action on Gaza. On April 15, 2026, he voted for two Sanders resolutions blocking arms sales to Israel and called the Netanyahu government's war illegal. In May 2026, he joined twelve Senate Democrats in a letter to CENTCOM questioning whether U.S. forces supported Israel's forced displacement of a million civilians in Lebanon. He has called for a Gaza ceasefire and condemned West Bank settler violence. At the same time, Luján voted in 2024 for the national security supplemental that included Israeli security assistance, and he has not called the campaign a genocide. He takes no money from AIPAC or United Democracy Project, though he has received funding from DMFI and other pro-Israel-aligned PACs. His votes and public statements show concrete steps toward blocking weapons transfers and holding U.S. military complicity to account, even as his record carries real contradictions that voters should weigh.

For the United States Senate in North Carolina, Michael Dublin is the strongest choice. His platform calls for drastic cuts to the U.S. military budget and opposes military intervention, and in March 2024 he publicly demanded that AIPAC be registered as a foreign agent while criticizing a fellow legislator for opposing a ceasefire in Palestine. He has not called the war in Gaza a genocide or voted against a specific arms-aid bill, and in a federal race that silence leaves the status quo of weapons transfers intact. Even so, no other candidate in this race takes a comparable position: Roy Cooper signed the SHALOM Act and rejected a legislative effort to block U.S. military aid to Israel, and Michael Whatley pledged unqualified solidarity with Israel at the Republican Jewish Coalition summit while drawing nearly $310,000 from pro-Israel PACs. Dublin's documented opposition to AIPAC's role, his insistence on a ceasefire, and his call to dismantle the war machine make him the only candidate in this field whose stated politics challenge rather than reinforce the machinery that keeps bombs falling on Gaza.

For the 2026 Ohio U.S. Senate race, Greg Levy (I) has published his positions on Palestine and AIPAC, making his stance on the conflict and the lobbying machine behind it publicly knowable. He has not yet called the assault on Gaza a genocide, cosponsored legislation to block arms transfers, or voted against military aid bills. As a candidate he has not cast those specific votes, and for a federal seat, the absence of blocking action leaves the status quo in place. The two other options have actively reinforced it. Jon Husted voted against discharging S.J. Res. 32 and 138 in April 2026, blocking floor votes to disapprove sales of D9 bulldozers and 1,000-pound bomb bodies to Israel, and has drawn over $645,000 from AIPAC PAC and United Democracy Project. Sherrod Brown voted for the April 2024 supplemental funding military aid to Israel and against all three November 2024 resolutions to block arms transfers, with his spokesperson affirming his commitment to funding Israel's war. Levy is the only option who has publicly opposed both the violence and the lobbying behind it rather than voting to fund it.

For the Oklahoma U.S. Senate race, N'Kiyla Jasmine Thomas is the strongest choice. She posted Free Palestine and pledged to call for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza, and she discarded a bin labeled AIPAC Funds, vowing to run as a grassroots candidate rejecting AIPAC and corporate PAC money. Thomas has not called the killing in Gaza a genocide and has not pledged to end U.S. military or economic aid to Israel; her platform calls for restoring USAID funding. Even so, she is the only candidate here both opposing the war and structurally cutting off the money that buys silence on it. Stinnett called the killing genocide and would vote against U.S. funding to Israel, but only until Netanyahu is replaced, tying his opposition to a foreign political outcome. Hern gave Israel full support to destroy Hamas and took nearly a hundred thousand dollars from AIPAC PACs in this race. Meinhardt opposed a U.S. war in Iran on Israel's behalf but has no stated position on Gaza. Thomas can deliver a ceasefire vote without waiting on a foreign government's leadership change, and she does it without AIPAC money in her war chest.

Voters choosing a United States Senator should back Jeff Merkley, who has taken concrete legislative action on both litmus tests. On November 20, 2024, he spoke on the Senate floor in support of three Joint Resolutions of Disapproval to block offensive weapons sales to the Netanyahu government, and in July 2025 he diverged from Senator Wyden on a vote to block arms sales to Israel. After a week-long Middle East visit, Merkley co-authored a twenty-one-page report with Senator Van Hollen in September 2025 calling Israel's Gaza actions ethnic cleansing and the United States complicit. He has not called it a genocide, and no divestment or broader aid-termination measure appears in his record. Still, among the candidates listed, Merkley is the only one with documented votes and floor action to stop weapons flowing to Israel. Libertarian Gary Dye's sole shown position is a single August 2026 social-media post condemning Zionist influence and U.S. support for the decimation of Palestinians, with no legislative action, floor speech, or vote. For a federal seat where silence upholds the status quo, Merkley's votes and floor speeches make him the clearer choice for voters who want arms sales to Israel actually blocked.

For the South Dakota seat in the United States Senate, Brian Bengs is the strongest option on the record. He has not called Gaza a genocide or voted to block weapons transfers, and in a federal race, no action on those questions supports the status quo. But he is the only candidate shown to place blame on U.S. policy: in June 2025 he called the United States partially responsible as Israel's primary weapons source, cited roughly two hundred American aircraft in strikes on Iran, and said Israel lacked legal grounds for those attacks. In September 2025 he published a legal analysis noting the U.S. supplied seventy-one percent of Israel's military aid and separated Netanyahu's government from the Israeli people. Mike Rounds, by contrast, voted in April 2026 against resolutions blocking roughly four hundred fifty million dollars in bulldozers and one-thousand-pound bombs for Israel, reaffirmed America's commitment to stand with Israel, and took in over one hundred seventy thousand dollars from AIPAC and UDP. Bengs names the armament pipeline and questions the legal case; Rounds defends both.

Rhode Island voters choosing their United States Senator in November 2026 should support Michael Bahry because he is the only candidate whose public statement directly challenges U.S. military funding to Israel. In August 2026, Bahry called for mercy over endless conflict and human dignity amid the suffering in Gaza, criticizing the flow of American weapons money into the war. Bahry has not called the war a genocide, has not backed a measure to block weapons transfers, and his humanitarian framing leaves the architecture of U.S. arms funding intact. Even so, his position is the clearest break from the status quo in this race. Jack Reed affirmed that U.S. commitment to Israel's security is ironclad, voted against blocking 1,000-pound bombs in April 2026, and accepted over $420,000 from pro-Israel PACs including AIPAC's United Democracy Project. Raymond McKay defends his association with the Republican Jewish Coalition rather than distancing himself from Israel-supporting organizing. Bahry is the candidate who has spoken against the machinery of this war rather than around it.

For the U.S. Senate race in Tennessee, Tharon Chandler is the strongest candidate on the question of Gaza. In a May 2025 post, Chandler explicitly called the Israeli war in Gaza a genocide, a word neither Marquita Bradshaw nor Bill Hagerty has used. Bradshaw's documented position is a diplomatic call for a two-state solution and meaningful policy changes by Israel, a framing that stops short of naming the crisis or condemning specific military actions. Hagerty voted against blocking arms sales to Israel in April 2026, drew AIPAC PAC's endorsement for opposing such measures, and framed the Gaza crisis as Hamas propaganda. On the second question, Chandler has not called for ending U.S. weapons or economic aid to Israel, and for a federal office-seeker that silence effectively supports the status quo of continued American military funding. Even so, among the candidates listed, Chandler is the only one who has named the atrocity for what it is and the only one who has not actively voted to keep the arms pipeline open.

James Talarico has not called the war in Gaza a genocide and has not backed ending U.S. military aid to Israel; his stated position is to condition that aid. But in this U.S. Senate race in Texas, his record is the strongest available. He has named Netanyahu's use of forced famine and collective punishment in Gaza, and at an October 2026 CNN town hall said Netanyahu has no right to wage war against civilians or restrict aid to them. He pledged not to take AIPAC money, and AIPAC did not endorse him in this cycle. Paxton, by contrast, opened a state Attorney General probe into pro-Palestinian student walkouts at Plano ISD, called for firing educators who facilitated anti-Israel rhetoric, and in October 2026 vowed to never stop standing with Israel and the Jewish people. Paxton took six thousand dollars from pro-Israel PACs; Talarico took four hundred fifty. For a federal office that shapes whether billions in weapons reach Gaza, Talarico is the only candidate on this ballot who has concretely condemned the methods Netanyahu has used against civilians.

Voters choosing their United States Senator in West Virginia need a candidate who will actually restrict the flow of American weapons to the war in Gaza. Rachel Fetty Anderson has not called the conflict a genocide or backed a specific vote to block arms transfers to Israel, but she is the only candidate here with a stated position: her campaign carries a dedicated Israel and Palestine page, she supports a two-state solution, and she says she would not vote to send or sell weapons to any country except in purely self-defense. That is a concrete restriction neither opponent has offered. Shelley Moore Capito cosponsored the 2025 Antisemitism Awareness Act, which directs the Education Department to apply the IHRA definition in campus investigations, limiting criticism of Israeli government policy, and her platform is silent on Palestine and Gaza. S. Marshall Wilson told a voter guide that Israel's worldview aligns more closely with the American Founding than any other Middle East nation and offered no statement on Palestine, Gaza, or U.S. regional policy. In a federal seat, taking no position supports the current arms and aid pipeline; Anderson at least draws a line on weapons transfers that Capito and Wilson have not.

For the U.S. House of Representatives seat in District 1, Monica Alponte is the candidate whose public stance most directly opposes the war in Gaza. In October 2026 she called the Gaza genocide by name and named U.S. officials Sullivan and Blinken war criminals. In September she pushed back against the Israeli UN delegation that sought to remove Palestinian children's drawings and argued that anti-Semitism is misapplied to Israel while Zionists are the true antisemites. Her campaign platform opposes U.S. military and financial aid to Israel and rejects AIPAC funding. She has not yet voted against an arms package or cosponsored a divestment bill, and as a federal candidate that platform commitment will be tested in committee. What separates her is that the other candidates go the other direction. Jay Feely has pledged to stand unapologetically with Israel and told Hamas it must accept a deal or face annihilation. Amish Shah, endorsed by Hindu American PAC, has supported Israel's war to destroy Hamas and U.S. Iron Dome funding. Neither has opposed the aid flowing to Israel. Alponte is the only candidate in this race whose statements center Palestinian lives and demand an end to American complicity.

Shomari Figures has not called the killing in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not taken specific legislative action to end U.S. military and economic aid to Israel. In a federal race, that absence of a stated position effectively supports the status quo. Even so, Figures is the stronger choice for this seat in the U.S. House of Representatives because a pro-Palestine organization has rated him an Ally, a designation his Republican opponent has no equivalent of. Rhett Marques has declared he is called to strongly support Israel as a Christian and American and has pledged to back the current administration's Middle East strategy, which in practice means continuing the very aid and arms flows that fuel the destruction in Gaza. Figures has not yet spoken or voted in the way voters need, but he is the only candidate in this race who has not committed himself to the pro-Israel establishment and remains open to the legislative action—blocking arms transfers, naming the killing for what it is—that the other candidate has already foreclosed.

Dr. Richard Pan has not called the killing of Palestinians in Gaza a genocide, and he has not voted to block U.S. weapons transfers or end military aid to Israel. In a federal race, taking no recorded position on those two questions effectively supports the status quo. But among the candidates on this ballot, Pan is the only one whose record tilts toward Palestinians. In September 2026 he condemned the U.S.-Iran war as a U.S. and Israeli attack that drove up gas prices, and in the August 17 Sacramento Bee debate he emphasized the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza rather than endorsing Israel's right to defend itself. CAIR Action lists him as its preferred candidate. His opponent, Kevin Kiley, traveled to Israel on an AIPAC-organized House delegation in April 2024, called the October 7 attack an act of barbarity and evil, praised Yale's overnight crackdown on pro-Palestine student encampments in April 2025, and collected $74,799 from pro-Israel PACs this cycle alone, including $39,000 from AIPAC's PAC. Kiley also voted five times not to stop the Iran war. Pan is the stronger choice for the U.S. House seat in California's sixth district.

For the November 2026 general election for the U.S. House seat in California's 22nd district, Randy Villegas stands apart from his opponents on the two questions that define this race. Track AIPAC documents that Villegas recognizes the genocide in Gaza and has pledged to oppose military aid to Israel. In January 2024, as a school board member, he signed a public ceasefire letter addressed to the Biden White House, and his campaign platform opposes the Iran war as a reckless war of choice. Pro-Israel spending groups DMFI PAC and 314 Action Fund both directed funds against him, while CAIR Action endorsed his general-election bid. By contrast, David Valadao co-introduced a resolution affirming Israel's right to defend itself after October 7, voted for emergency military funding to Israel, and received AIPAC PAC endorsement for this race. Villegas is the candidate who has taken concrete, public action on stopping the war and cutting off arms, rather than the one whose record is built on supporting the very aid and military operations that have fueled the destruction in Gaza.

Voters choosing for the United States House of Representatives seat in CD-3 should look to Clifton Brown, whose 2026 campaign platform names the US-backed attack on Gaza a genocide, pledges to stop funding Israel, and commits to ending US arms sales worldwide. Brown is the only candidate whose position assigns the United States direct responsibility for the conflict through its funding and weapons policy. Dwayne Romero supports continued US military funding for Israel from a defensive perspective, keeping American weapons flowing regardless of civilian harm. Jeff Hurd called the Israel-Hamas ceasefire a critical turning point for peace while attending an AIPAC-organized trip to meet Prime Minister Netanyahu, and in 2026 received over $100,000 from AIPAC PAC and United Democracy Project. Vote for Peace, which rates candidates on human rights and war-lobby alignment, opposes Hurd. Brown has not yet voted on a floor bill or cosponsored specific legislation, but his platform is the only one in this race that names the genocide and pledges to end US funding and arms transfers.

For the U.S. House of Representatives, Manny Rutinel is the strongest choice. In 2022 he called Israel's actions in Gaza a genocide and urged an early ceasefire, grounding his stance in his Palestinian heritage. That is a concrete, first-person opposition to the war. On the second test, his record contains no vote against arms funding, no cosponsorship of a weapons-transfer block, and no divestment action; as a federal candidate, taking no recorded position on aid effectively endorses continued U.S. military and economic support for Israel. His campaign drew roughly $200,000 from a fund that received United Democracy Project money in 2024, and he took $18,100 from pro-Israel PACs in this cycle. Even so, he is the only candidate here with a stated, dated condemnation of the genocide. Gabe Evans introduced a resolution in June 2025 to label the Free Palestine slogan antisemitic, posted in October 2026 that he stands with Israel, and collected over $68,000 from AIPAC's PAC. Vote for Peace, a Muslim-community-aligned group, opposes Evans. Rutinel's shortcomings are real, but Evans's record is one of shielding Israel and suppressing pro-Palestinian speech.

For the U.S. House of Representatives seat in Michigan's 4th district, Shafina Barnett is the strongest candidate on Palestinian justice. Barnett is a confirmed member of the pro-Palestine Muslim community, a standing alignment with anti-Zionism that neither opponent matches. Barnett has not voted on arms-funding bills, cosponsored a weapons-transfer block, or formally labeled Gaza a genocide; in a federal seat, the absence of a recorded position on these questions carries the weight of the status quo. She is nonetheless the best option here. Bill Huizenga voted in April 2024 to advance H.Res. 1117 shielding Israel from one-sided pressure on Gaza, and in May 2024 voted for H.R. 6090 embedding the IHRA framework in federal education law. Sean McCann's platform is silent on Israel and Palestine; in August 2026 he said he would take a look at military aid to Israel without committing, and his campaign is backed by Israel-aligned labor unions including the AFL-CIO, AFSCME, and AFGE. Barnett carries a confirmed community commitment to Palestinian justice that neither McCann's equivocation nor Huizenga's pro-Israel votes can match.

Sam Forstag is the strongest candidate for United States Representative in this district because he has taken a concrete, dated stand on the two questions voters are being asked to weigh. On May 24, 2026, Forstag publicly stated that he would not vote for an appropriations package sending weapons to Israel and called the situation in Gaza a genocide. That single statement does two things at once: it names the killing for what it is and it puts him on the record against the specific funding mechanism that keeps American munitions flowing to the campaign. No other candidate in this race has a researched record on these issues, and in a federal seat where silence functions as a vote to continue the current course, Forstag's willingness to say, on a named date, that he will not fund the weapons and that the killing is a genocide makes him the clear choice for a voter who wants their representative to break the status quo rather than preserve it.

For this House race, William Lawrence has repeatedly and personally labeled Israel's attacks on Gaza a genocide—at a Latino community forum on June 16, 2026, in social-media posts, and as a core campaign credential. His platform calls for stopping arms sales to Israel and pursuing diplomatic solutions rather than military escalation. On June 22 he challenged opponents to answer whether Israel committed genocide, and by July 24 his opposition to the genocide and the war in Iran was central to his campaign, prompting DMFI to spend roughly one million dollars against him through Rolling Sea PAC. Vote for Peace rated Lawrence an Ally. He has not cosponsored specific legislation or cast a legislative vote, but his stated platform directly addresses both the genocide and U.S. arms transfers. His opponent Tom Barrett declared in October 2024 he will always stand with Israel, urged Michigan State to adopt the IHRA definition of antisemitism, and has taken over seventy thousand dollars from pro-Israel PACs including AIPAC and the Republican Jewish Coalition. Vote for Peace opposed Barrett. Lawrence is the candidate who names the genocide and opposes the weapons pipeline.

For the United States House of Representatives seat in North Carolina's 11th district, Jamie Ager (D) stands as the only candidate in this race with a documented pro-Palestinian alignment. Vote for Peace, a Muslim-community and pro-Palestine-aligned organization, placed Ager in its Ally tier based on the candidate's human rights positions and war-lobby funding profile. Ager has not made a public statement calling the war in Gaza a genocide, has not cosponsored a bill to block weapons transfers to Israel, and has not voted to end U.S. military or economic aid to Israel. For a federal office-seeker, the absence of action on these questions effectively upholds the status quo of unconditional aid and arms support. Ager's case rests on broader human rights positions and resistance to war-lobby influence rather than on direct legislative or public commitments on Palestinian justice, which makes Ager the strongest documented option for voters who want a representative oriented toward accountability while still pressing for concrete action on Gaza once in office.

Denise Powell is the only candidate in this race for U.S. House of Representatives with a recorded stand against pro-Israel political money. In April 2026 she rejected support from the super PAC Democratic Majority for Israel, and in May she disavowed all Israel-focused outside groups, prompting DMFI to cancel its Nebraska ad buy. On the two questions that matter most to voters—opposing the genocide in Gaza and ending U.S. military and economic aid to Israel—Powell has not called the violence a genocide, cosponsored a bill to block weapons transfers, voted against arms funding, or backed divestment. For a federal office-seeker, that absence effectively leaves current U.S. support for Israel in place. Among the candidates listed, she is still the one who publicly turned away pro-Israel PAC backing and made that disavowal a matter of public record. It is also notable that AIPAC-backed United Democracy Project organizations, including BOLD America and EDW Action Fund, continued to spend in her support even after her disavowal, and DMFI had planned its ad buy before canceling it. She is the sole candidate in this race with a researched record.

In the November 2026 general election for the New Hampshire 1st House seat, Stefany Shaheen is the stronger choice. In August 2026 she backed the Massie Amendment to block U.S. military aid to Israel and built her primary campaign on an anti-AIPAC platform, attacking opponent Sullivan over donations from 150 AIPAC supporters and framing AIPAC-linked giving as disqualifying. She also donated $29,650 from AIPAC-adjacent donors to three New Hampshire community health centers. Shaheen has not called the war in Gaza a genocide. Still, among the candidates on this ballot she is the only one who supported cutting off military funding to Israel and who treated AIPAC-linked money as disqualifying. Anthony DiLorenzo stated at the August 2026 GOP primary debate that he supports Israel, offering only narrow humanitarian conditions as a qualifier, and his campaign drew an AIPAC-linked FEC donation. Shaheen's concrete backing of the Massie Amendment and a campaign that centered opposing AIPAC influence make her the clearest break from the status quo in this race.

In the race for the New Jersey seventh congressional district, Seamus O'Toole is the only candidate who names what is happening in Gaza by its actual term. Running under the Stop Israel's Genocide Party banner and identifying as an anti-genocide independent, O'Toole has made explicit genocide language the center of his campaign, opposing Israel's conduct throughout 2026. He has not voted to block weapons transfers to Israel or advance divestment. But neither opponent has come close. Thomas Kean Jr., endorsed by AIPAC, voted yes on the fourteen-billion-dollar Israel Security Supplemental containing no Palestinian humanitarian aid and voted yea on the IHRA education-discrimination bill, framing the conflict around October 7. Rebecca Bennett, backed by J Street PAC, took over eighty-five thousand dollars in pro-Israel contributions and ran a campaign whose international section addresses China while never naming Israel or Gaza beyond one humanitarian-aid plea. In a federal race where silence on genocide and aid functions as support for the status quo, O'Toole is the only candidate who has refused to look away.

For the U.S. House seat in CD-2, Teresa Benitez-Thompson is the clearest choice for voters who want concrete pressure on American policy in Gaza. Her platform conditions U.S. military aid on Israel's compliance with international humanitarian law, phases out offensive arms sales, ends settlement expansion, and directs funding to UNRWA within a two-state framework. She has not called the war a genocide and still funds Iron Dome, stopping short of ending all military assistance. Even so, no other candidate here offers a comparable architecture that ties continued aid to enforceable legal standards and channels resources to Palestinian civilians. David Flippo carries an AIPAC endorsement, blamed Hamas for Gaza's humanitarian crisis on a July 2025 broadcast, and states no Israel or Palestine policy of his own. His October 2026 claim that his nonprofit delivered food to Israel was contradicted by records showing the Order of St. John made that delivery. A federal candidate who takes no position effectively supports the status quo; Benitez-Thompson at least conditions it.

Gabriel Vasquez is running for a U.S. House of Representatives seat. On the two questions voters weigh first — opposing the genocide in Gaza and ending U.S. military and economic aid to Israel — Vasquez has not called it a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not supported divestment. For a federal office-seeker, taking no position on those questions supports the status quo of continued arms flows and aid to Israel. The one vote he has shown in this space is a Yea on H.R. 6090, the Antisemitism Awareness Act, which writes the IHRA definition into Title VI education-discrimination enforcement and treats anti-Zionism as antisemitism in schools, placing him in the pro-Israel bloc of the House. That is a real, checkable record, and in a race where he is the only candidate with one, voters get a representative whose votes they can find and hold him to. If transparency and accountability in a federal office is what you want, that is the strongest option on this ballot.

For the U.S. House seat in Ohio's 15th district, Don Leonard has staked a clear position where his opponent has not. In an April 2026 interview he weighed calling Israel's conduct in Gaza an act of war, crimes against humanity, or genocide, and by October 2026 the AIPAC Tracker noted that he rejects AIPAC and the Israel lobby outright and supports a full arms embargo on Israel. Vote for Peace rated him an Ally on these questions. Mike Carey, by contrast, took over $92,000 from AIPAC's PAC and its super PAC United Democracy Project in 2026, voted in favor of the Antisemitism Awareness Act in 2024, and cosponsored a pro-Israel antisemitism resolution in May 2025. When Carey called for ending the Gaza war in October 2025, he framed it solely as a response to the October 7 Hamas attack. Vote for Peace opposed him in the general. For a voter who will not accept the status quo on Gaza, Leonard's stated arms-embargo position and his naming of the killing as genocide put him ahead of a candidate whose funding and votes remain locked to the Israel lobby.

For the U.S. House seat in the 7th district, Brian Poindexter offers the clearer break from Israel-aligned politics than Max Miller. Poindexter has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not voted against Israel aid bills. What he has done is frame the conflict as a military issue, telling voters in August 2026 that Miller fights for Israeli soldiers to get the benefits that our military members get, and his campaign platform calls for ending the Iran war to lower energy prices. He has backing from Congressman Ro Khanna, a Muslim-community and pro-Palestine-aligned member. By contrast, Miller calls himself a proud Jewish American and a staunch defender of Israel, co-led the reintroduction of the Antisemitism Awareness Act in February 2025, and took in over $473,000 from pro-Israel PACs including AIPAC and its super PAC United Democracy Project. Poindexter's pro-Israel PAC total was roughly $29,000, chiefly from J Street. In a federal race, silence on blocking aid and naming the situation effectively supports the status quo, but Poindexter's stated opposition to regional U.S. military escalation and his framing of Miller around Israeli military benefits make him the stronger choice.

Marlon Duran is the strongest choice for Texas's 28th congressional seat because he is the only candidate who has broken the funding structure that buys silence on Gaza. In March 2026 he pledged never to accept money from AIPAC, foreign interest PACs, corporate PACs, or any PAC, and his platform frames the Palestinian struggle in anti-apartheid terms, calling for international law rather than alliance loyalty. He has not cosponsored measures to block weapons transfers or end military aid, and has not called the killings in Gaza a genocide; in this office, that silence leaves the aid and arms pipeline untouched. But Cuellar, who welcomed the October 2025 peace deal as relief and hope, voted in 2026 to defund colleges that boycott Israel, and took over a million dollars in pro-Israel PAC money including over $907,000 from AIPAC, and Tijerina, who cheered U.S. strikes on Iran and pledged America stands shoulder to shoulder with Israel, are both locked into the status quo. Duran's refusal of the money that shapes those votes is a concrete act of opposition to the machinery behind the war.

Vote for Bob Brooks for U.S. Representative in Pennsylvania's 7th district. Brooks has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and has not voted against U.S. aid to Israel; his platform addresses economy, healthcare, immigration, and climate but is silent on Palestine. For a federal office-seeker, taking no recorded position on these questions effectively supports the status quo of American military and economic support for Israel, and he did receive $87,773 from pro-Israel PACs. A human-rights and war-lobby funding assessment nonetheless rates him as an Ally, which is directional evidence of alignment with Palestinian justice even though he has not cast a recorded vote or issued a statement on the issue. Ryan Mackenzie, by contrast, sponsored the Iran Sanctions Act, voted Yea on the Illegitimate Court Counteraction Act in January 2025, and drew $99,653 from AIPAC PAC and United Democracy Project within $130,103 in pro-Israel money, then credited the president in October 2025 for ending hostilities and called it a new day for the region. Brooks is the stronger choice because he has taken no recorded pro-Israel action while Mackenzie has taken several specific ones.

For United States Representative in Texas's 34th congressional district, Eddie Espinoza is the only candidate who has explicitly named Netanyahu's war in Gaza a genocide, urging voters to vote peace. In October 2024 he accepted the Fort Bend County Anti-Genocide Pro-Palestine coalition's recommended-candidate slate, citing his Palestine advocacy, and in June 2026 he publicly called the war a genocide while accusing AIPAC of controlling both of his opponents. He has not on the record backed blocking weapons transfers or ending U.S. military and economic aid to Israel, and in a federal seat that absence of action effectively supports the status quo on arms shipments. Still, he is the only candidate listed who has spoken the word genocide, aligned himself with a local pro-Palestine coalition, and explicitly rejected the AIPAC alignment he says drives his opponents. His stated position makes him the strongest available choice for voters who need a representative that will not pretend the killing in Gaza is not what it is.

For the U.S. House race in Virginia's 5th Congressional District, Tom Perriello is the stronger choice. He has not called the war in Gaza a genocide or voted to block weapons transfers to Israel, and in a federal seat that silence effectively upholds the current military and economic aid relationship. What he has done is commit his platform to credible sanctions against genocide and human rights violations and, in June 2023, state that tools to combat antisemitism cannot be repurposed to silence academics and advocates speaking in support of Palestinian human rights, a position with pro-Palestine-aligned directional backing. His opponent John McGuire traveled to Tel Aviv in August 2025 on an AIEF trip, the AIPAC congressional branch, during the ongoing Gaza war, met Netanyahu, and urged him to get the job done in Gaza. McGuire also amplified Laura Loomer posts framing Gazans as a threat to Western civilization. One candidate defends the speech of those advocating for Palestinian rights while pledging sanctions against atrocities; the other urges a prime minister to keep bombing and echoes dehumanizing rhetoric about an entire population. Perriello is the clear choice.

For the U.S. House seat in Virginia's First District, Shannon Taylor (D) is the stronger candidate, though her record carries real limitations. Taylor has not called the war in Gaza a genocide and has not backed blocking weapons transfers; when asked in October 2026 about an arms embargo she declined to endorse or reject aid, offering only that assistance must comply with international law. At a September 2026 rally she was asked about Palestine and did not answer. For a federal office-seeker, that inaction effectively supports the status quo. Even so, Taylor is the better choice against Robert Wittman (R). On October 7, 2024, Taylor called for an immediate ceasefire, hostage release, and rebuilding plan, naming innocent lives lost in both Israel and Gaza. Wittman signed an October 2025 letter opposing Ireland's import ban and ICJ genocide-redefinition efforts, framing both as targeting Israel. He also voted yea on the Antisemitism Awareness Act in May 2024 and sponsored its companion in February 2025, embedding the IHRA definition in federal education law. Taylor's willingness to name Palestinian suffering distinguishes her from a candidate whose record centers on shielding Israel from international accountability.

For the U.S. House seat in Wisconsin's 3rd District, Rebecca Cooke is the stronger choice. In October 2025, Cooke called on the United States to halt arms to Israel, a direct demand to end the weapons pipeline fueling the campaign in Gaza. In October 2023, she stood with all civilians and branded Van Orden's trip to Israel a renegade trip rather than a solution. She has not called the war a genocide, and she drew nearly $250,000 in pro-Israel PAC spending in her favor this cycle. Even so, her public call to stop American arms flows marks her as the only candidate here pushing against the military relationship. Van Orden voted Yea in May 2024 on H.R. 6090, the Antisemitism Awareness Act, which embeds the IHRA definition into federal education-discrimination enforcement, and Vote for Peace rated him Opposed in this cycle. His record aligns with Israel-centric positioning rather than Palestinian justice. Cooke's escalating positions, civilians first and then arms halt, put her ahead where the other option votes to lock the IHRA framework into law and takes no step toward stopping weapons.

For the California State Assembly seat in AD-11, Jenny Leilani Callison is the strongest choice. On July 26, 2026, she publicly accused Israel of carpet bombing Lebanon, killing people, and stealing land for Greater Israel, and she stood firm defending Palestinian claims when critics pushed back. She has not called the situation a genocide or demanded an end to U.S. military aid to Israel. But among the candidates in this race, Callison is the only one who has taken a concrete public stand against Israeli military actions and territorial seizure. Lori Wilson, by contrast, voted Aye on AB 715, California's antisemitism coordinator and classroom-oversight bill, and her only pro-Palestine signal is a CAIR Action general-election Preferred listing, a tier below full endorsement. Callison's willingness to name what is happening and defend Palestinian claims puts her clearly ahead in a race where voters need an Assembly member who will not look away.

Scott Sakakihara is running for California State Senate District 10. He has not called the war in Gaza a genocide and has not backed blocking weapons transfers or U.S. aid to Israel. What he has done is push Union City in 2024 to consider a Gaza ceasefire resolution and advocate an ethical investment policy, and his state-senate platform addresses housing, healthcare, immigration, and climate. CAIR Action listed him as a general-election preferred candidate, and Muslim Democrats and Friends Club of Alameda County endorsed him. That Muslim-community backing, combined with his willingness to put a ceasefire question before a city council, positions him as the candidate in this race most responsive to the community demanding an end to the killing, even as his platform does not yet name a foreign-policy stance on Israel.

For the California State Assembly seat in district 14, Mark Rendon is the candidate whose platform most directly confronts the crisis in Gaza. He names the situation in Palestine a genocide, demands California divest state funds from complicit corporations, adopt BDS standards for all state expenditures, and repeal state laws barring educators from teaching about the genocide. Vote for Peace rates him an Ally in this general election, and BDS sits at the center of his policy agenda as a concrete demand. The alternative, Buffy Wicks, voted aye on AB 715, which creates a state antisemitism coordinator and imposes classroom-material oversight, and after the October 7 attack she called the violence terrorism plain and simple and said she stands with the Israeli people. Democrats for Israel California endorsed Wicks at its Support tier. Rendon moves from naming the violence to demanding specific financial and legislative changes in how California spends and educates, while Wicks's classroom oversight vote and public solidarity with Israel place her on the opposite side of the questions that matter most here.

Matt Haney has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and has not taken divestment action. He remains the strongest option for the California State Assembly seat AD-17. In February 2026, Haney invited children from Gaza through HEAL Palestine's Global Healing program to speak on the Assembly floor in Sacramento about their treatment, a concrete act of centering Palestinian voices inside the legislature. He holds endorsements from CAIR Action and AROC Action, and he voted aye on SB 403, the caste bill, in 2023. His demonstrated willingness to bring Palestinian suffering directly into the Assembly chamber and his alignment with Muslim-community organizations give voters a clear basis for support in this race.

For the California State Assembly, District 18, Mia Bonta (D) has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not taken divestment action. What she has done is push back where it mattered: when AB 715, the antisemitism-coordinator and classroom-material oversight bill whose floor debate centered on speech about Palestine, passed in a late-night session, Bonta was named a skeptic and pressed the bill's co-authors to clean up its text. She ultimately voted aye, and that vote counts against her. Still, her documented skepticism and pressure on the bill's authors, combined with Vote for Peace rating her an Ally and both CAIR Action and AROC Action putting their names behind her, mark her as the candidate in this race who has actually engaged with the question of Palestinian speech rights in the California legislature. No other candidate here has a researched record to compare against, and Bonta's combination of a relevant pushback on AB 715, her positive standing on the Palestine-speech question, and Muslim-community-aligned backing makes her the strongest choice on the list.

For California State Assembly District 20, Liz Ortega (D) carries endorsements from CAIR Action and AROC Action, organizations that assess candidates on Gaza and ceasefire positions, signaling that her record meets their standards on Palestinian rights. Ortega has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not cosponsored a measure to block weapons transfers to Israel, and has not taken a documented legislative stand on the conflict. Her one recorded vote touching on these issues was an abstention on AB 715, a bill establishing an antisemitism coordinator and classroom-material oversight, where no Aye or No was logged. She did vote aye on SB 403, a caste-equality measure, in 2023. In a race where documented positions on Palestinian rights are scarce, Ortega is the only Assembly member with directionally pro-Palestinian community endorsements, and that distinction is the clearest signal available to voters on these litmus-test issues.

Alex Lee is the only candidate in this State Assembly 24th-district race with a researched record, and it shows consistent, dated action on Palestinian solidarity. In October 2023 he called for a ceasefire to protect children in Gaza. In August 2025 he backed Ro Khanna's call for U.S. recognition of Palestinian sovereignty. In April 2026 he endorsed Tom Steyer for governor because Steyer would stand against AIPAC. CAIR Action and AROC Action endorsed his general-election bid. To be clear, Lee has not called the war in Gaza a genocide and has not voted to block weapons transfers or cut aid to Israel. He also abstained on AB 715, an antisemitism-coordinator bill, without stating a reason, and in June 2023 he co-signed a letter urging a pause and further study of SB 403 before voting to pass it. Among the candidates on this ballot, Lee is the one who has taken concrete steps toward Palestinian rights and positioned himself against AIPAC influence, making him the strongest choice for voters who want a representative accountable to the Palestinian community.

For California State Assembly District 25, Ash Kalra is the strongest option. In January 2025 he publicly drew a parallel between LA wildfire-displaced residents and Palestinians, urging empathy for both groups, and in September 2025 he coauthored SCR 105, a resolution calling for the end of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza and the immediate release of all hostages. That is concrete legislative action on the crisis. Kalra has not called the violence a genocide or backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel. Even so, he has a documented record of taking both legislative and public stands alongside Palestinian suffering, and both CAIR Action and AROC Action have endorsed him, signaling that Muslim-community leaders view his work as aligned with their community's needs. His 2023 decision to publicly press the author of a caste-protection bill on why the language was necessary, then vote to support it, also shows he will push back on majorities when conscience demands it.

Voters for Alabama governor should choose Doug Jones because he has taken the clearest stand against the destruction in Gaza of any candidate in this race. In November 2024 he named Israeli actions a genocide and declared that America must stop funding the killing, and in September 2026 he called for force rather than mere sanctions to end what he called Israel's genocide in Gaza and Lebanon. On the two questions that matter most—naming the killing and ending U.S. financial and military support—Jones has answered yes in direct, dated statements. Vote for Colt Shelby for Arkansas governor. Shelby has not called the killing in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons shipments, and has not pushed divestment from Israeli bonds. He has, however, publicly rejected the state's Israel-first posture, calling Governor Huckabee's Israel pledges and the renaming in Israel a distraction from Arkansas families facing food insecurity and infant mortality. Fredrick Love, as state senator, sponsored Resolution 60 commending Israel and affirming an unqualified right to defend itself, shielding the state from any accounting for Palestinian harm. Sarah Huckabee Sanders has made Arkansas a fiscal partner of Israel, committing $25 to 50 million in Israeli government bonds, cementing an unbreakable bond with Netanyahu, signing legislation embedding IHRA definitions into public schools, and calling it disgusting to question Israel's conduct in Gaza. Shelby is the only candidate who has refused to treat alignment with Israel as beyond criticism, and the only one whose platform—state contracts, education, criminal justice, energy—prioritizes Arkansas over foreign-policy theater.

For California governor in the 2026 general election, Xavier Becerra is the stronger choice. He has not called Israel's actions in Gaza a genocide and has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and Vote for Peace rates him neutral rather than an ally. But his record still sets him apart: at the 2024 World Health Assembly he called for a ceasefire agreement, hostage release, more humanitarian aid for Gaza, and a path to a two-state solution; in a 2026 gubernatorial debate he called the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran illegal; and in May 2026 he demanded international accountability for Netanyahu's conduct.
