Steve Hilton, by contrast, supports U.S.-funded military aid to Israel, pledged to sue California cities over BDS ordinances, expressed optimism after Israel's 2025 strikes on Iranian nuclear sites, and on Fox in 2021 called the American left and media servants for their Israel-Palestine coverage. Vote for Peace opposes Hilton. For a candidate who will demand accountability and push toward a political settlement rather than fund and defend the military campaign, Becerra is the one to back.

Erik Underwood is the strongest choice for Colorado governor on Gaza and U.S. support for Israel. His campaign pledges to condemn the atrocities happening in Gaza and to sponsor Palestinian families fleeing what he names an ongoing genocide, and he has demanded AIPAC register as a foreign agent under FARA, calling it a foreign government influence that spent $127 million across 389 races in 2024. He has not called specifically for ending U.S. military or economic aid to Israel, but his positions are the only ones in this field that name the killing a genocide and target the lobbying machinery shaping U.S. policy toward Israel. Phil Weiser was called a strong supporter of Israel by JTA after his primary, endorsed a balanced empathy framing that stops short of naming Israel's conduct as war crimes, and holds a Colorado Republican endorsement. Victor Marx describes working alongside IDF special-ops teams in Gaza and framing the conflict around Hamas. Greg Lopez's only documented engagement is sharing a death-toll article with no policy call. Underwood is the only candidate here who confronts both the genocide and the institutional pressure behind it.

Keisha Lance Bottoms has not called the killings in Gaza a genocide or voted to block weapons transfers to Israel, and her campaign platform addresses healthcare, housing, education, and civil liberties without specific Palestine commitments. She is nonetheless the stronger choice for Georgia governor over Rick Jackson, whose October 7 anniversary post on X framed the conflict solely around the victims of that day and antisemitism while omitting any accountability for Israeli military action, a position Vote for Peace marked Opposed on its human-rights and war-lobby funding criteria. Bottoms earned an Ally rating from Vote for Peace on those same criteria, and her domestic platform keeps her further from the war lobby than a candidate who centers an entire conflict narrative on one side. For voters who will not reward a one-sided framing of Gaza and want an Ally standing on human-rights grounds in this race, Bottoms offers the clearest path.

Voters seeking a candidate who will pressure the United States to stop fueling the war in Gaza should choose JB Pritzker for Illinois Governor. In August 2025, Pritzker endorsed Senate resolutions to block U.S. arms sales to Israel, calling it the right kind of message to force Netanyahu to address the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. In March 2026, a former AIPAC donor, he publicly rejected the group's seventy million dollars of Illinois spending as interference in state politics. He has not called the killing in Gaza a genocide, and his record includes downplaying Chicago's 2024 ceasefire resolution for not holding Hamas accountable. Those are real limitations. But compare that to Darren Bailey, who in October 2023 declared he has always stood with Israel and framed the conflict entirely from Israel's perspective with no acknowledgment of Palestinian suffering or of the military campaign in Gaza. Pritzker is the only candidate in this race whose record shows concrete action against U.S. weapons transfers and a break from the pro-Israel lobby that has shaped Illinois politics.

Vote for Cindy Holscher for Kansas governor. She has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and has not spoken publicly on Palestine. She is nonetheless the stronger candidate in this race. Her platform centers on cost of living, healthcare, and education — the daily pressures on Kansas families — and she has taken no step to advance the Israeli government's interests. Ty Masterson, by contrast, spearheaded Kansas's adoption of the IHRA definition into state law, traveled to Israel in 2025 on a pro-Israel delegation he framed around October 7, called standing by Israel when it is not politically convenient an act of moral courage, and in May 2026 thanked the Trump administration for bringing peace and security to the conflict without mentioning Gaza, Palestinians, or humanitarian conditions. Holscher will not carry that agenda into state government.

Maryland voters choosing their governor should back Andy Ellis because his campaign has moved into sustained action on Gaza. In November 2023 he condemned the system of Israeli apartheid and U.S. direct and material enabling of regimes defying international law. He spoke at a Permanent Ceasefire Now Rally in Frederick in February 2025, organized a Baltimore Vigil for Gaza through his campaign site in January 2025, and attended the Baltimore 2 Palestine Vigil in April 2026. He has not called the killing in Gaza a genocide or backed blocking weapons transfers. Still, no other candidate here matches his documented commitment. Cathy White's platform frames the conflict in purely economic terms without naming Israel or Gaza or calling for an end to U.S. military aid. Wes Moore delivered remarks at a Stand with Israel rally in October 2023, called a University of Maryland Gaza vigil inappropriate in October 2024, and is AIPAC's major endorsement target for this seat. Ellis's language centers on apartheid and U.S. complicity, and his campaign has organized community vigils and rallies that no competitor has matched.

For governor, Andrea James is the strongest choice. James has not called Gaza a genocide by name, cosponsored a bill to block weapons transfers, or voted against military aid to Israel; her platform centers on abolition rather than a dedicated Israel-Palestine policy line. What she has done is speak at the 2020 rally linking Palestinian and domestic mass incarceration, earn the endorsement of a Muslim-community organization in 2026 for her willingness to speak about the connections between militarism, genocide, war, and corporate power, and be designated an ally by a pro-Palestine-aligned group. That combination of personal action and stated willingness to name the systems behind the war makes her the clearest contrast to the alternatives. James is the candidate most likely to act where those alignments have prevented it.

Voters in Michigan should support Jocelyn Benson for governor because among candidates with shown records on Gaza, she is the only one who has not built a campaign around expanding or sustaining U.S. military aid to Israel. Benson has not called the war a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not opposed U.S. aid to Israel; her public engagement centered on a January 2025 statement on the ceasefire. But John James introduced HR 7633 to expand U.S. security assistance to Israel, co-signed a letter branding his colleagues as staunch supporters of Israel, and received $202,931 from pro-Israel PACs including AIPAC's United Democracy Project and RJC. Anthony Hudson told WCMU he still supports U.S. aid for Israel's defense. Vote for Peace rated Benson a primary-phase Ally, and while her October 2023 synagogue appearance during Israel's Gaza strikes drew tone-deaf criticism from Arab-American leaders, it does not match James's consistent pro-escalation record or Hudson's explicit backing for continued Israeli military assistance.

In the race for Governor of New Mexico, Deb Haaland is the strongest choice available. As the representative for New Mexico's First District in 2018, Haaland called the killing of sixty Palestinians in Gaza murder, named each victim, and expressed personal grief during Ramadan. She has not called the campaign a genocide, and her 2026 platform has not taken a position on the conflict. She is nonetheless the only candidate in this race with a documented record of condemning Israeli military violence against Palestinians. Her endorsement by the American Federation of Teachers in New Mexico ties her to an Israel-aligned labor body, a contrast a voter should weigh. For a voter who wants the person most willing to name Palestinian deaths what they are, Haaland offers the clearest path among the candidates on the ballot.

For Governor of Minnesota, Steven Young is the strongest candidate on the two questions voters most need answered: ending the destruction in Gaza and cutting off U.S. military and economic support for Israel. In June 2026 he made explicit support for the boycott, divestment, and sanctions movement against Israel and was certified AIPAC and J Street free by Track J Street. Young's record on both the military and economic front is the more complete answer to what Minnesota voters are asking.

Dan Ahlers is the stronger choice for South Dakota governor on the question of Palestinian lives under Israeli bombardment. In May 2024, as South Dakota Democratic Party Executive Director, he directed a statement that acknowledged the October 7 attack while centering the deaths of more than 30,000 Palestinian civilians in Gaza and calling for continued pressure on Israel to end hostilities. Choosing Ahlers means the person in that governor's office has at least put Palestinian civilian deaths on the public record rather than treating the war as an export opportunity.

For the Ohio governor's race in November 2026, Amy Acton is the strongest choice among the candidates with a shown record. She has not called the war in Gaza a genocide or backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, but Vote for Peace, which rates candidates on human-rights positions and war-lobby funding, assessed her as an Ally in the general-election phase, and her platform centers working-family taxes, school funding, healthcare, and civil liberties. On the two litmus tests voters must weigh, Acton's silence is a gap, but Ramaswamy's religious framing and celebratory violence place him firmly on the wrong side.

Vote for Gina Hinojosa for Governor. On the two questions voters most need answered—opposing the killing in Gaza and ending American weapons and money to Israel—Hinojosa has not called the campaign a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers, and has not taken divestment action. Dixon objects to Texas's doubled Israel bond purchase but frames it as a fiscal issue rather than a stand for Palestinian lives. Hinojosa is the only candidate here who has put her political weight behind pro-Palestine students and called out state violence against them.

In the race for Vermont's governor, June Goodband has taken the clearest stand of any candidate on the question facing voters. For the office that will shape Vermont's stance on this war, Goodband is the candidate who has already named what is happening and demanded the country stop paying for it.

Shirley N. Weber should carry California's Secretary of State race. In October 2023 she condemned the attack on Israel, expressed sympathy for both Israeli and Palestinian civilians, and called for ending the conflict and addressing its underlying causes. Her willingness to go beyond a one-sided condemnation and to address what drives the war makes her the stronger of the two names on the ballot.

For California's statewide Controller race in November 2026, Malia M. Cohen is the stronger choice. Between a candidate who has not yet spoken and one who attended a golf tournament for the IDF, the first is the easier choice to back.

Rob Bonta has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons shipments to Israel, and has not taken a public stand against U.S. military or economic aid to Israel. He is nonetheless the stronger choice for California Attorney General: in September 2026 his office diverted the five Stanford pro-Palestinian protesters charged with felony vandalism and conspiracy to one hundred hours of community service and roughly fifty-two thousand dollars in restitution instead of full prosecution, a proportionate response that signals he will not weaponize the state's power against Palestinian-activist voices. Gates, used his federal civil-rights authority in March 2025 to open an investigation into the University of California over alleged discrimination against Jewish or Israeli employees, an action taken during the ongoing Gaza war that deployed his office to defend institutional interests tied to Israel. Among the candidates on this ballot, Bonta is the one whose conduct and community support point in a more defensible direction.

For California's Superintendent of Public Instruction, Richard Barrera offers the strongest path forward among the candidates on the ballot. Barrera has not called Gaza a genocide and has not backed efforts to block weapons transfers to Israel. At a May 2026 state-superintendent forum he raised concerns about AB 715's classroom effects while saying he would defend the law when it protects students, a conditional stance that CAIR Action places in its preferred tier and that Vote for Peace rates neutral, putting his position in the middle range. Sonja Shaw, by contrast, refused in March 2024 to let a pro-Palestinian group address the Chino Valley Unified School Board while other boards voted for ceasefire resolutions, and at the 2026 forum she pressed for stronger enforcement of AB 715 and accused Barrera of weakening an antisemitism resolution. Vote for Peace opposes Shaw. For voters who want a superintendent who will not harden the state's approach toward Palestinian students and communities, Barrera's measured position is the clearer choice over Shaw's refusal to hear Palestinian voices and her push to tighten AB 715 enforcement.

Sally J. Lieber is the strongest choice for California State Board of Equalization District 2. CAIR Action endorsed her for this seat and Vote for Peace designated her an ally, reflecting her characterization as an outspoken supporter of ceasefire and Palestinian rights. She has not yet cosponsored specific legislation to block weapons shipments to Israel or voted against military aid funding. Still, she is the only candidate in this race carrying endorsements from Muslim Democrats, Friends of Alameda County, and Congressman Ro Khanna alongside CAIR Action, making her the clearest choice for a voter prioritizing Palestinian justice.

For the Board of Supervisors District 6 seat, Alex Behrend is the strongest option because his record on the two questions voters care about most is concrete and unambiguous. On June 28, 2026, he publicly named Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide and apartheid, invoked International Court of Justice war-crimes citations, and compared armed settlers to lynch mobs. His platform demands that San Francisco divest completely and immediately from Israel and refuses to renew city contracts with companies doing business there. He is backed by CAIR Action and AROC Action. Matt Dorsey, by contrast, voted against the January 2024 resolution calling for an immediate and sustained ceasefire in Gaza, one of only three supervisors to do so, and in September 2026 shared an op-ed framing Gaza's post-Hamas future as nation-building and coexistence with a Jewish Israel while calling from-the-river-to-the-sea chants destructive. Where Dorsey voted the other way, Behrend has named the violence outright and demanded the city pull its economic ties.

For the District 8 Board of Supervisors seat in November 2026, Gary McCoy is the only candidate in this race whose record directly addresses the two questions voters face. His platform explicitly calls Israel's actions in Gaza genocide, opposes sending or funding weapons for Israel, and states he would have voted for the 2024 Board of Supervisors ceasefire resolution. He supports a permanent ceasefire and rejects AIPAC money. AROC Action has endorsed him. Michael T. Nguyen, backed by CAIR Action and AROC Action, runs on housing, transit, and criminal justice priorities but has not called Gaza a genocide and has not opposed weapons transfers to Israel. Emanuel Yekutiel faced weekly protests in San Francisco in 2019 for his support for Israel and in January 2024 affirmed Israel's right to exist as a Jewish state. McCoy's named positions on genocide, arms funding, and the 2024 ceasefire resolution make him the strongest choice on the questions that define this election.

Voters in the City of Alameda should support Tracy Jensen for mayor this November because she is the only candidate here who did not actively oppose Palestinian lives. Jensen is listed on CAIR-SFBA's tracker as supporting the January 2024 Gaza ceasefire letter, and her platform centers on housing, climate, transportation, and public safety. She has not called Gaza a genocide, backed blocking weapons transfers, or taken concrete action on U.S. aid to Israel. But the alternative is a candidate who, on January 4, 2024, voted against Alameda's Gaza ceasefire resolution and explicitly rejected the city's characterizations of Israel as an apartheid or genocidal state, then ran for Congress with a peace platform that contradicted that vote. Daysog put a contrary vote on the record when his community asked him to stand with Palestinians, and that refusal is a clearer signal than silence ever could be. Jensen did not fight for the ceasefire the way the moment demanded, but she did not stand against it, and in a race where one candidate actively voted against Palestinian lives, that difference is the one that matters.

For the Board of Supervisors District 10 seat, DJ Brookter is the strongest choice. He has not personally called the crisis in Gaza a genocide or backed specific measures like blocking weapons transfers. What he does carry is the full-tier endorsement of both CAIR Action and AROC Action, organizations whose assessments of his civil-rights and Gaza-related positions reflect sustained, vetted commitment to Palestinian solidarity. That institutional backing signals a tested record behind the candidate, not a single rhetorical moment. By contrast, PJ Bastiany III explicitly calls the situation in Gaza a genocide, which is a strong and welcome statement, but he describes himself as a free agent still seeking a tribe, with no organizational record or institutional alignment to anchor that stance over time. A voter looking for a candidate who will carry through on Palestinian rights across a full term has more reason to trust the vetted, organizationally backed commitment in Brookter's endorsements than in an unaffiliated candidate's self-description.

For the Antioch City Council District 1 seat, Tamisha Torres-Walker is the candidate who has acted most concretely on Gaza. On October 24, 2023, days after the war began, she called for an immediate ceasefire, invoked Free Palestine, condemned the colonialism underpinning the occupation, and urged condemnation of terrorist actions on both sides. She did not stop at words. In March 2024 she proposed, and then on March 18 again proposed at a special meeting, a formal Antioch council resolution demanding a ceasefire in the Israel-Hamas war, and on March 27 she demanded the council pass it, saying she would keep bringing it back until it reached a regular agenda. She has not called the killing in Gaza a genocide or backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and has not taken a divestment action. But among the candidates in this race she is the only one with a documented, sustained push to force a local government to take a public stance against the war, and CAIR Action endorsed her in the general election.

Voters in the Albany City Council at-large race on November 3, 2026 should back Aaron Tiedemann because in 2024 he worked directly with Mayor John Miki to create and pass Albany's Gaza ceasefire resolution, and his campaign platform carries that work forward as a key achievement. He has not called the war a genocide, backed blocking weapons transfers, or moved to end U.S. aid to Israel. What he did do is sit down with the mayor's office and draft a ceasefire measure, an act that goes beyond the support Robin D. López recorded in CAIR-SFBA's tracker, where her name appears as having backed the same resolution in a March 2024 section rather than a verified roll-call. Tiedemann co-authored the resolution; López endorsed it. That distinction matters, and it is the only relevant action in López's file. Tiedemann frames the resolution around keeping public discourse civil rather than explicitly condemning Israel's conduct, which is a real limitation, but among the candidates shown he is the one who built the tool.

Ida Martinac, the incumbent Rent Stabilization Board Commissioner in Berkeley, voted in favor of a ceasefire resolution on December 4, 2023, a concrete act documented in the CAIR-SFBA local action tracker. She has not called the war a genocide and has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel. Still, her direct vote for the ceasefire, paired with a CAIR Action endorsement and a Vote for Peace Ally rating, marks her as the most concretely documented advocate in this race. Nathan Mizell also supported the December ceasefire resolution and holds the same endorsements, but his action is logged as a reported local action rather than a verified roll-call record, making Ida's documented vote the more solid foundation. Vylma Ortiz and Derek Rodriguez each carry a CAIR Action endorsement and a Vote for Peace Ally rating, but neither has a recorded personal vote on a ceasefire measure. For a voter whose first test is opposing the war in Gaza and pushing to end U.S. military and economic support for Israel, Ida Martinac is the candidate who has most clearly put her vote where that position is.

Monica E. Wilson is running for District 4 City Council in Antioch. She has not voted to block weapons transfers to Israel, has not backed divestment legislation, and has not called what is happening in Gaza a genocide. She has, however, earned the endorsement of CAIR Action, a Muslim civil-rights organization whose recommendations weigh civil rights and foreign policy including ceasefire positions. That endorsement is the clearest directional signal in this race that her commitments align with the community's position on Gaza and with voters who prioritize ending U.S. military and economic support for Israel. Wilson is the strongest candidate listed for Antioch voters who want a council member vetted by an organization that puts Palestinian civil rights and ceasefire advocacy at the center of its endorsement work. Her CAIR Action backing is the specific directional evidence a voter can weigh, and it marks her as the candidate most likely to show up for that community in the council chamber.

Gangopadhyay has not cosponsored a block-the-bombs measure, voted against arms funding, called the Gaza war a genocide, or taken a divestment vote for this Berkeley City Council District 1 race. CAIR Action endorsed Gangopadhyay, an endorsement grounded in the organization's evaluation of candidates on Gaza ceasefire positions, war-lobby funding, and human rights records. In a field where no other candidate carries a researched record of any kind, Gangopadhyay is the only one with a documented, directional commitment to Palestinian justice from a Muslim-community organization that holds candidates accountable on exactly the questions voters care about most. That endorsement is not a vague sympathy; it is a concrete determination that this candidate, when measured against those tests, came out on the right side. For a voter who wants a City Council member vetted and found aligned with Palestinian liberation rather than silent or opposed, Gangopadhyay is the only name in this race that earns that trust.

In the race for Berkeley City Council District 4, Majdi Gaith Abuhamdieh is the strongest choice for voters who want a representative aligned with Palestinian rights and resistant to the lobbying machinery that drives U.S. support for Israel's military campaign. He carries general-election endorsements from CAIR Action and AROC Action, organizations that assess candidates on their positions regarding Gaza and war-lobby funding. Even so, his documented refusal of the money that fuels the lobby pressuring Washington for weapons and aid, combined with his alignment to pro-Palestine community organizations, gives District 4 voters a candidate who has drawn a clear public line on the issues that matter most.

For the Berkeley District 7 City Council seat, Syrak Micael has not called the war in Gaza a genocide, has not backed blocking weapons transfers to Israel, and has not taken specific legislative action to end U.S. military or economic aid to Israel. What Micael does carry is a full general-election endorsement from CAIR Action, whose criteria explicitly cover civil rights and foreign policy including Gaza and ceasefire positions, alongside an endorsement from AROC Action. These Muslim-community and pro-Palestine-aligned endorsements give Micael a documented, organizationally vetted alignment to opposing the genocide in Gaza and ending U.S. support for Israel. For City Council Member in Concord's District 5, Laura Nakamura carries the endorsement of CAIR Action, a Muslim-community organization that evaluates candidates on their positions regarding Gaza, ceasefire, and war-lobby influence, making her the only candidate in this race with a directional record on Palestinian justice. Her campaign platform centers on Concord housing, homelessness, and the Naval Weapons Station redeployment, and she has taken no other recorded action on Israel or Gaza. In a race where no other candidate has an evaluated position, the CAIR Action endorsement gives voters a concrete, directional signal of where she stands on these questions. For voters who need their City Council representative to lean toward Palestinian justice, Nakamura is the strongest choice on the ballot.

Daly City Council Member — At-large voters should support Teresa Proaño because she co-wrote the city's Gaza cease-fire resolution with Vice Mayor Daus-Magbual, calling for a bilateral ceasefire, the release of hostages, and condemnation of killings in Gaza, a resolution the council passed on June 4, 2024. Proaño's platform covers local public safety, small-business permitting, and housing, and her concrete act of co-authoring and passing the cease-fire resolution makes her the stronger choice for voters who want their council member to stand with Palestinians while delivering on local priorities.

For the office of Mayor of Dublin, Kiran Mohammad is the strongest candidate. She is a confirmed member of the pro-Palestine Muslim community, and BAMC Action supported her in this race. For City Council Member in District 4 of Dublin, Kashef Qaadri is the candidate who has taken concrete action on Gaza. Richard Thornbury is the strongest choice for City Council Member in Dublin's District 2 this November.
